Uniform Title: *Troṭalātantra* Manuscript: NGMCP Manuscript No.: 5-4852 Reel No.: B 126/9 Description: Description by Mark S.G. Dyczkowski.

Troṭalā is another name for the goddess Tvaritā, whose visualized form is described in verses 1.28–59. She is called Troṭalā because she shatters (troṭana) bondage; she is called Tvaritā because her vidyā acts with speed.

(*Travṛtā*). She is not a well-known goddess nowadays, yet there is evidence that she was more popular in the past; thus, she is well known to the *Kubjikā* Tantras prior to the twelfth century. Her association with Kubjikā is also [evident].

This is implied in this Tantra by identifying her with Kubjikā as Trikaṇṭhikā (1/94). This Tantra contains details of her worship both externally and inwardly as the prāṇa rises, in the course of which she ascends through...

She breaks through the barriers and attains union with Bhairava at the summit of her ascent. She is associated with ghosts and demons—such as *gūhyakas*, *piśācas*, *yakṣas*, and so forth—of whom she is said to be the sovereign (*īśvarī*); thus, her *vidyā* and her worship [are described].
They also serve as means for exorcising and controlling them.

*Troṭalamahātantra*, p. 1a.
Oṃ, salutations to Śiva!
To the Supreme Lord, seated upon the peak of Kailāsa, the sovereign of all worlds, the creator of everything from Ananta down to Śivā; (1)
Formless, supremely peaceful, the delight of Pārvatī’s heart, the expounder of all scriptures, and praised by all the perfected ones (siddhas). || 2 ||
It is worshipped by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Mahendra, and other gods, as well as by the Dānavas; it is served by Skanda, Nandin, the Gaṇas, and many others numbering in the tens of millions.
It was likewise well-worshipped by the ṛṣis and others such as the gandharvas, and highly praised by the siddhas, vidyādharas, yakṣas, and rākṣasas.
It is eternally surrounded by the Nāgas beginning with Ananta and ending with Kulika;
it is crowded with throngs of Apsarases and highly praised by the daughters of the Siddhas.
Some praised the Lord of Gods, some danced before him; some sang the Sāman chants, while others stood with their heads bowed in prostration.
There, some praise him with hymns while others scatter flowers;
they laugh, shout "kilikila," roar, and leap up.
Therein there is no death, no old age, no disease, and no suffering;
thus beholding Śiva, who is joyfully exultant and honored by the best of gods.
Having prostrated himself like a staff upon the ground, with his knees touching the earth and his palms joined in reverence, Tārkṣya spoke these words.
O Blessed One, God, Lord of Gods, Savior from the ocean of saṃsāra!
O Lord, tell this most secret question to me, your devotee. (10)
It is the supreme among tantras and the most excellent among mantras;
therein reside various and manifold accomplishments in brief. (11)
By this, one attains liberation, and independence arises;
as well as the accomplishment of sovereignty and the fulfillment of other purposes. (12)
There are various sports of the *nāgas* as well as the removal of poison;
and the fierce *yakṣa*-seizures, fevers, *lāmās*, *śākinīs*, and *pūtanās*. (13)
The Kuṣmāṇḍas, Yakṣas, Vetālas, and the exceedingly powerful Daityas, as well as the subjugation and summoning of Bhūtas, Pretas, and Piśācas; || 14 ||
Practitioners on the surface of the earth desire to attain the state of moving through the air (khecaratva),
as well as the supernatural powers of the earth and the netherworld (mahīpātālasiddhi), along with the sword, collyrium, and sandals.
How is it that the pill, the cloth, the great weapon, the supreme paralyzing of nooses, their severing, their burning, and the various initiations [are explained]? (16)
How can there be immediate departure [from the body] in both spiritual authority and liberation? And how can there be the entry of one's own self or that of another into the body of another? (17)
How is it that there is the extinguishing of fire without flames, and how is the seedless state [of consciousness] achieved?
Likewise, how do the burning and the nourishing of both the stationary and the moving occur? (18)
How can a jar, fire, water, a treasury, or a pillar of poison [be animated]?
How can there be an immediate possession of wood, stone, or living beings? (19)
By what ritual action are diseases such as leprosy destroyed?
[It is] the cutting of the spells of others and the protection of one's own knowledge of the Self. (20)
The acquisition of a field, how the protection of that field may be achieved, the pinning down of an enemy kingdom, as well as its sowing with dissension and its deluding; || 21 ||

The slaying of Māra, the proclamation of Māra, the accomplishment of the state of a universal monarch (cakravartin), and the power to assume any form at will in the state of a sky-farer according to one's own desire.
O Śaṅkara, you have fully explained all this— the camel-herd of the celestial, aerial, and terrestrial Yoginīs— to me, your devotee.
For a thousand divine years, you were propitiated by me through ascetic penance;
therefore, O one of great austerity, Brahmā has arrived—choose a boon!
Brahmā said:
"O Lord of Birds, since you are incapable of these tasks, I declare that knowledge alone is supreme; go to Kailāśa, into the very presence of the Lord. (25)
When the Great Ascetic was pleased, Īśvara granted him a boon;
then, with a mind drawn [toward it], he approached the Lotus-born One.
"O Lord of the Gods, tell me this which is my desired boon;
for the sake of the welfare of practitioners, be intent upon bestowing grace. (27)
The Lord said:
O Lord Garuḍa, listen to this supreme truth concerning that matter:
formerly there was a most terrible and excellent form of Bhairava. (28)
Emerging from my body were many innumerable beings born of yoga, possessing fierce forms and delighting in blood, flesh, and corpses. (29)
Insatiable, greedy, terrible, and always assuming fierce forms—
for the sake of testing them, I [bestowed] upon them knowledge born of yoga.
And being impelled by my state as a sacrificial animal, I have been earnestly entreated:
"O Lord of the Gods, preside over the rites involving the *caru* oblation within the maṇḍala. (31)
"I have empowered it, and I have said: 'I have gone to the summit of Mount Meru;
there is a city named Vajrārgala, constructed there from five kinds of jewels. (32)
In the center is an eight-petaled lotus with a radiant yellow pericarp;
there are vajras in the four cardinal directions and a vajra-enclosure in the intermediate directions.
There were gates and pathways, with an exit through the southern gate;
there, I stood in the center of the pericarp, fierce with the power of my strength.
Having meditated upon the supreme power, Akṣobhyā, who is most immutable,
[he remained] on the peak of Kailāsa for that long, urged by Gaurī’s joy.

O Goddess, where was that Blessed One Rudra situated when he was established in the state of a sacrificial animal (paśu), requested by the Yoginīs for the purpose of the caru-offering while remaining within the maṇḍala? || 36 ||
Then Gaurī, blazing with the brilliance of ten million lightning bolts, became enraged;
she was the swift and rapid Vidyā, empowered by the three seed-syllables and the three qualities (guṇas).
Resplendent like a mass of lightning, pervading all that is moving and stationary,
she illuminates the ten directions with many millions of throbbing rays of light.
By that blazing mass, the gods beginning with Brahmā were paralyzed; they uttered cries of "Alas! Alas! and cried out, "Save us, O Goddess, beloved of Śiva! (39)
Having arrived at the base of his feet, they praised him with excellent hymns;
she, being pleased by those various hymns characterized by [references to] her head, feet, and other limbs, [listened]. (40)
For each single syllable of the Goddess, two arms are proclaimed;
thus the Goddess has eighteen arms and is seated upon the lion-throne of Dharma.
Glorious, white as cow's milk, with the brilliance of a great tail, possessing a lolling tongue and a most fierce mouth, with large, quivering, sharp fangs. 42.
With blazing eyes, most terrible, with stiff ears and very fearsome,
roaring, powerful, and formidable, with flaming, curled hair. (43)
With his sharp and formidable claws extended, tearing apart the worlds,
he stood facing the east, blazing as if swallowing all that is moving and unmoving.
Tvaritā has mounted there, with her left leg hanging down and her right leg doubled back, placed upon the top of her foot.
The nails of the Goddess's feet shine like shimmering stars;
they possess the reddish hue of a lotus and are marked with the sign of a lotus.
Beneath her feet shine long, well-proportioned toes;
her shanks are well-rounded, her thighs are full, and the expanse of her hips and thighs is broad.
Her navel is deep, her three folds and the line of hair are beautifully adorned;
her waist is broad, and her breasts are like golden jars.

She had a neck like a conch, lips like the bimba fruit, and eyes like the petals of a blue lotus; she possessed six faces, full lips, and eighteen eyes; she had a beautiful nose, eyebrows curved like a bow, lovely ears, and was radiant with a crown. (49)
Resplendent with flashing jewels, possessing the brilliance of a thousand hoods,
the King of Nagas was made into a necklace, while she shone with earrings.
The two arms of the Goddess shine, their beauty enhanced by the coils of serpents;
likewise, her waist is adorned with a girdle fashioned from a great serpent.
The two terrible anklets on the goddess’s feet are made of serpents;
she has placed her left foot upon a thousand-petaled lotus.
One garment shone like a flash of lightning, adorned with flowers,
while another garment was made like a rainbow, covering her breasts.
The goddesses, with weapons held in their hands and sharp-pointed claws like oyster shells, bound the great serpent with firm knots using many flowers.
She has made weapons of her right hands: the vajra, the staff, the sword, the discus, the mace, the flaming trident, the arrow, and the spear, as well as the gesture of granting boons. 55.
In her left hands, she holds a bow, a noose, a bell, a raised index finger, a conch, a goad, and likewise a lotus, while displaying the gesture of fearlessness. 56.
Resembling a thousand flashes of lightning and filled with quivering rays, they covered the domain of Śiva’s thunderbolt with their own splendors. 57.
Urged on, they hasten with speed; O terrifying one created by the syllable *hūṃ*, these deities of the difficult terrain, hard to behold, threaten all the directions. (58)
The circle of Yoginīs is deluded and has fainted upon the summit of Meru;
it has fallen and is withering away—save it, O Goddess, Sovereign of the Gods! 59.
Having praised her with various hymns, and having performed half of the *oṃkāra* rite for me,
I worshipped that goddess and prostrated before the Yoginī. (60)
O Lord of the Gods, restrain this very wheel of yoginīs against me!
Stay, stay, O greatly radiant one, here in the center of the maṇḍala! || 61 ||
Having entered the mandala, the goddess sat upon the pericarp,
honored with various garlands, perfumes, incense, and offerings.
Having praised her many times with hymns accompanied by mantras and mudrās, the practitioner who remembers the Goddess established in the pledge (samaya) [attains success]. || 63 ||
She herself will grant him the desired accomplishment without delay;
and the *yoginīs* who roam the earth shall bestow upon him the fulfillment of all his desires and aims. (64)
Gods, Daityas, along with Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Uragas, and Apsarases,
grant you the fulfillment of your desires through your swift worship.
But he who constantly worships [the deity] at home with devotion according to his own capacity—
his enemies go to destruction, turning their backs even upon their desired objects.
When worshipped, he conquers foreign kingdoms with ease;
moreover, there arise abundant prosperity, health, and long life.
All tasks, both divine and non-divine, are accomplished in many ways.
In the meantime, Brahmā arrived at the summit of Mount Meru.
Having worshipped according to this rite and praised him many times with hymns, he was honored by Viṣṇu, as well as by Vāsava, Agni, and Yama. (69)
Nairṛta, Varuṇa, Vāyu, and Dhanada were there, as well as Īśāna; and Umā-devī was present with the Siddhas and the hosts of Daityas and Apsaras. (70)
Honored and praised, the goddess, satisfied and joyful in mind, said:
"O Lord of Gods, I shall do so for that man who remembers me. (71)
"I shall grant him his desired accomplishment without delay.
Then Brahmā asked about the means of accomplishing the Vidyā. (72)
Then they were all dismissed after this supreme tantra was spoken:
"The *Troṭala*, O Bird, is the supreme secret, consisting of one hundred thousand verses plus a quarter-lakh. (73)
Having thus summarized that which is the most essential of the essential, I shall now speak of the supreme secret; listen, O Kamalā! (74)
O Tārkṣya, the supreme Vidyās established therein consist of nine seed-syllables;
that Vidyā is supremely secret, more secret even than the secrets.
It is the supreme secret lore of the Guhyakas, the means for accomplishment that fulfills all desires;
it is the crusher of all Nāgas and the bringer of destruction to the faction of enemies. (76)
She is proclaimed as the destroyer of all wicked beings;
she is the agitator of those women who are both divine and non-divine.
She is proclaimed as the source and the origin of all seeds;
she is the heart of all goddesses, residing within the hearts of the Yoginīs. (78)
This vidyā accomplishes all rites throughout the entirety of the worlds;
it bestows success in all undertakings, both in this world and in the next. (79)
She is difficult to attain even for all the goddesses, the ṛṣis, and the yogins;
indeed, those such as the munis and vidyādharas who have attained perfection in kalpa after kalpa [cannot reach her]. 80.
Indeed, this single Mistress of Vidyās instantly terrifies all yakṣas, rākṣasas, piśācas, as well as pretas and bhūtas.
"Ta-la-ti" refers to the seven netherworlds (pātālas), while "jvālāgni" refers to the regions up to the edge of the universe;
beginning with the vowel "oṃ," it denotes everything up to the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa). || 82 ||
Because it protects from everything and indeed causes all things to tremble, it is called Troṭalā; this is the established meaning of the tantra. || 83 ||
This vidyā was perfected in ancient times; it bestows accomplishment even upon those devoid of knowledge, even without the practice of vows, and even without a guru or ritual sacrifice.

Not discerning what ought to be done from what ought not to be done, and not knowing what is authoritative from what is not, they perform terrible deeds and become even the destroyers of the gods. (85)

Furthermore, impelled by the command of the Lord of Gurus, men in this mortal world perform sacrifices and other rites; yet they suffer on account of their prior actions, both auspicious and inauspicious. (86)

By means of which they quickly attain accomplishment and go to liberation, both supreme and secondary; and those who desire the state of a Vidyādhara or even the status of a Cakravartin [attain it]. 87.
Mortals seeking curiosity perform the sport of the *nāgas*,
desiring to attain the power of moving through the sky together with the masters of perfected yoga (*siddhayogeśvara*). (88)
They desire death at their own will as long as Lord Sadāśiva [is propitiated]; he bestows the perfection of sovereignty—what then to say of the perfection of wealth? (89)
One certainly performs actions such as summoning through the mind alone—namely, killing, driving away, subjugation, cutting, and likewise burning. (90)
It causes the division of enemy armies and the destruction of foes;
it deludes all the wicked and provides protection to those afflicted by fear. (91)
Whoever recites this knowledge even once,
the Goddess, the God, and Garuḍa— this triad— reside within his body.
Known as Trikaṇṭaka, there shall be a presence of the triad;
they are established within the three systems of Vāma, Dakṣiṇa, and Siddhānta.
This vidyā, renowned as Trikaṇṭakā, grants all desires;
it is accomplished swiftly, and for that reason it is called Tvaritā.
Thus ends the first chapter in the *Tvaritāmūlasūtra* of the *Ādyatroṭala*. 1.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the *prastāra* (the mystical diagram), which is difficult to obtain on earth even for the Siddhas,
Gandharvas, Devas, Sages, Yakṣas, and great Serpents.
O Lord of Garuḍa, [this teaching] was formerly protected by Brahmā and the other gods from the Dānavas;
it should be performed on a very level stretch of ground, strewn with heaps of flowers. (2)
In a smooth and delightful place, free from hair and bones,
one should draw the Mātṛkā there, accompanied by the designations of its groups (vargas).
O Tārkṣya, because practitioners understand the extraction of mantras through this [system],
I have therefore proclaimed it with such effort at the beginning of the nomenclature.
By which the great net of mantras radiates throughout the ten directions;
the first group of vowels consists of sixteen syllables in measure. (5)
Others consist of five groups of five syllables each, and two others consist of four syllables each;
this first group of vowels has been proclaimed by me at the beginning of the groups.
In the palatal group, the second [consonant] is produced at the palate; the third is produced by the tongue and the palate;
the fourth is at the palate; the fifth is at the tip of the tongue; and the fifth [of the dental group] is produced by the tongue and the teeth.
The sixth is the group consisting of the sibilants and the letter *ṣ*; the seventh is the mixed group;
and the eighth is said to be the aspirates (*ūṣman*); thus they have been described to you, O Lord of Birds.
O Bird, the supreme Goddess, who consists of nine seed-syllables and bestows all accomplishments, remains undestroyed when extracted by means of the *prastāra* grid.
O Tārkṣya, I shall now extract this vidyā together with its defining characteristics,
using the secret seed-syllables and vowels that are hidden at the end of the Mātṛkā.
O Lord of Birds, the seed-syllable beginning with the root-vidyā is said to be mounted on the sixth vowel, ending with the sibilant (ūṣman) and accompanied by the bindu. 11.
The second letter of the palatal class joined with the eleventh vowel; the union of the tongue and palate constitutes the first armor. (12)
One should then apply that same second [syllable] below;
it is joined with the eleventh vowel and is the first [consonant] from the palatal group (tālavya). (13)
One should join the second of the sibilants (ūṣman) below that [first sibilant], conjoined with the sixteenth vowel;
then the third of the sibilants [is joined] with the sixteenth vowel.
In the conjunction of the tongue and the teeth, one should first apply [the sound] from below;
then the second [letter] of the mixed group (miśravarga) from below once again. 15.
Combined with the first letter of the palatal class (tālavya) and conjoined with the fourth vowel, one should place the second letter of the sibilants (ūṣman) below it. 16.
The eleventh vowel, conjoined with the final of the sibilants (ha) and the bindu, mounted upon the fifth vowel, through the union of the lips in a closed position. || 17 ||
The second syllable is another, [formed] by the union of the tongue-tip and the palate;
the first [syllable] is to be joined with the fifth [consonant], and these have been extracted by means of half a vowel. 18.
This great vidyā is swift and bestows all accomplishments; one should always recite the mantra joined with the syllable Oṃ at the beginning and "namas" at the end. (19)

In rites pertaining to Agni, [the mantra] ends with *svāhā*; now hear [also] regarding the limbs (*aṅga*). The fourth vowel, surmounted by a nasal dot (*bindu*), is joined with the sibilants (*ūṣman*) at the end. (20)
In the second [chapter], the *Miśravarga*, one should place the *ūṣman* at the end;
it should be seated upon the sixth vowel and adorned with dots (*bindu*) above its head. (21)
The first syllable, devoid of the bindu and adorned with the sixteenth vowel, is declared to be the heart; the sibilant (ūṣman), however, becomes twofold.
The wise one should cause the first [syllable] to be joined with the second;
joined with the sixteenth vowel and repeated twice, it becomes the head.
In the conjunction of the two lips, there is the second [consonant] joined with a bindu, combined with the fourth vowel, situated within the two mixed groups [of consonants]. (24)
Upon the union of the tongue and the palate, there is the third letter from the mixed group;
it is mounted by the fourth, and again, the third of the mixed group.
The five-syllable crest-mantra (śikhā) is known to be joined with a double repetition;
it is conjoined with the fifth vowel, the final of the sibilants (ūṣman), and the bindu.
Furthermore, that third mixed group should be applied purely;
once it has been mounted there, one should again apply the first [group].

The five-syllable armor-mantra consists of the sibilants ending with *ūṣman* (the letter *h*) together with the bindu; it is mounted upon the first of the mixed [vowels], and then again the first of the sibilants.
The second seat of the mixed [deity] is joined with the bindu;
it is the second of the sibilants (ūṣman) conjoined with the first of the palatal group (tālavya). || 26 ||
The wise one should cause the second letter of the mixed [group] to be joined with a bindu;
furthermore, the second, fourth, and sixth vowels should be applied in sequence. (27)
O Bird, know that the three eyes are produced from the seeds of the Sun, Moon, and Fire;
they should be joined in sequence from the right, the left, and upwards. (28)

Having joined the palate-group (tālavya) and so forth with the second of the sibilants (ūṣman), the second of the mixed group (miśravarga) should be joined to the fourteenth and the fifteenth [vowels]. || 29 ||
Below that, having joined the sixteenth vowel up to the end of the *ūṣman* sounds, one should then add the second letter of the palatal class (*tālavya*) conjoined with the *visarga*. (30)
The fifth vowel joined with the last of the sibilants and the bindu—
this four-syllable weapon-mantra is interlaced with the syllable *phaṭ*.
The trident, sword, discus, and arrow are thus proclaimed;
one should place them in the east, south, west, and north respectively.
Furthermore, each individual weapon and this entire collection is very difficult to conquer;
these secret limbs, O Tārkṣya, were guarded by Brahmā in ancient times.
Without these, there can be no accomplishment in this *Troṭalottara Tantra*. It should be guarded with great effort and not be given to one who has not been tested. (34)
Now listen attentively as the ancillaries of the Vidyā are being proclaimed:
the Ādividhṛdaya is declared first, and it is held to have three or four heads. (35)
The fifty-fifth and fifty-sixth [syllables] are declared to be the *śikhā*; the seventh and eighth are the *kavaca*.
The *tārakā* becomes the *netra*, while the nine-and-a-half-syllable [mantra] is the *rakṣaṇa*. || 36 ||
O Tārkṣya, listen to how the female messengers (dūtīs), the mantras, and others are situated:
having written "hūṃ lalala," the vajra-tuṇḍa then comes into being.
By joining with *khakhehū*, the ten seed-syllables are proclaimed;
she is known as Vajratuṇḍā, the messenger of Śakra, possessed of great power. || 38 ||
Having written "khecara jvālinī," one should employ it with the word "jvalati.
Combined with "khakheta," this Jvālinī is truly terrifying. (39)
Agnidūtī is greatly radiant; having extracted [the mantras] by means of the ten seed-syllables and having inscribed Carceśvarī, Bhīṣaṇī then arises.
This very Vidyā named Śavarī, consisting of ten syllables, should also be applied; she is proclaimed as Yamadūtī, the one of great power. (41)
The word *chechedanī* should be joined, and immediately after that, *karālī*.
Then *khagaccha* should be joined again, followed by *karālī* and *ugrarūpiṇī*. (42)
This messenger of the southwest, possessing ten seed-syllables and great power, is as follows:
having written *kṣaḥ*, *śrava*, *dravaṃ*, *saṃ*, and *likhya*, the syllables *plavaṅgī*, *śroḥ*, and *kṣaḥ* are extracted. (43)
The ten-syllabled Plavaṅgī is indeed the messenger of Varuṇa;
having written "strīcalā," one should likewise write "kalā" and "dhūnanī. (44)
The *rāstrī* should be joined together, and the ten seed-syllables (*bīja*) are extracted. This is the *manovegā-vidyā*, the messenger of Vāyu, possessed of great power. (45)
By adding *kṣa* to *kapila* and then placing *hasaya* after it, this ten-syllable vidyā named Kapilā is extracted. (46)
The Yakṣadūtī is most terrifying, both gentle and fierce, possessing a divine form;
she is proclaimed as HŪṂ Tejovatī Raudrī Māte HŪṂ. || 47 ||
Rudradūtī is the Great Fierce One, named Raudrī, possessed of great power;
this ten-syllable mantra is proclaimed as Rudradūtī. (48)
Having written "pharephaghne," one should apply "phe cakre.
Indeed, this Viṣṇudūtī, joined with "pharepha," is of great power. (49)
The ten seed-syllables are thus specified; Cakravegā indeed bestows all desires.
Having inscribed [the syllables] upon a fierce and terrible wooden board (khaṭṭa) where the letters are difficult to pronounce, one should likewise write "duḥ" and "tathā."
These ten seeds are proclaimed as the excellent messengers of Brahmā;
she is named Brahmavetālinī, most terrible and exceedingly fierce in her power.
O Lord of Birds, these ten seed-syllables have been declared in this Troṭala;
from them, thousands of vidyās have emerged in manifold ways.
The essence has emerged from them; here, the quintessence of essences has been extracted.
This collection of mantras is perfected; cast aside anything else like chaff.
Thus ends the second chapter in the *Tvaritāmūlasūtra*, the first [part] of the great tantra *Troṭala*.
Now I shall explain another [method]; listen with a one-pointed mind, O Bird!
The two hands should be purified with the Astra-mantra, submerged within one another. (1)
Facing north, the mantra-practitioner should employ the *tarjanī-astra* (the threatening weapon-gesture);
he should perform three resounding claps and threaten the directions with his index finger.
The practitioner of mantra should recite the weapon-mantra while placing the left [hand] on the left side and the right [hand] on the right side; the right [hand] above and the left [hand] below.
Having empowered it with the secret weapon-mantra (guhyāstra) and likewise with the knowledge-weapon-mantra (vidyāstra),
the reciter of mantras should place them upon his hands and in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
One is not overcome by gods, nor by dānavas, nor even by obstacles;
having first placed the secret limb, one should place the heart in the youngest [limb].
The head-mantra is to be joined with the thumb and ring finger; the crest-mantra with the middle fingers;
the armor-mantra is to be joined with the index finger; and one should place the eye-mantra upon the palm of the hand.
The weapon of the index finger (tarjany-astra) should be applied again, and likewise the limbs of the Vidyā;
and the female messengers (dūtīs) should also be applied, starting from Jyeṣṭhā and facing forward.
O Six-faced One, one should place the five Vidyās behind [the image];
furthermore, one should place the Root Vidyā upon the fingernails and shells.
Then one should perform the placement (nyāsa) upon the bodies both in reverse and in direct order:
beginning from the feet up to the head, and beginning from the head down to the feet.
Having placed the secret limbs (*guhyāṅga*) according to their respective locations as prescribed,
one should then place the limbs of the Vidyā and apply the garment of the directions (*digvastra*).
From the feet, knees, thighs, and private parts, up to the navel, heart, throat, and palate,
and from the water-pot (vata) to the top of the head— both downward and upward— from the primordial seed-syllable.
The practitioner of mantra should place the seeds beginning with Durjaya in the locations as described;
at that very moment, all obstacles, both external and internal, will be destroyed.
Thus, purification of the body occurs both externally and internally;
one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) as prescribed, and thereafter, perform the internal rite.
The practitioner should visualize that syllable Oṃ, which has the form of the moon and rains down a stream of nectar, entering through the aperture of Brahmā (the *brahmarandhra*). 14.
Having formed a fist with the left hand, one should place the thumb facing downwards on the head, face, throat, heart, navel, genitals, thighs, knees, and shanks. (15)
The practitioner of mantra should repeatedly place the primordial seed-syllable on the thumb and the other fingers;
he should then apply the seed-syllables as the limbs upon the fingers as they have been described.
With five [syllables], one should perform a salutation and place the form of a lotus below;
above the moon and below it is the lotus, the body whose nature is the seed-syllable.
He who knows it in its true nature becomes eternally immortal;
for him there is neither death nor old age, neither disease nor indeed any harm-doers. (18)
And one quickly attains accomplishment both in this world and in the next.
Having formed the shape of wings with the hands, one should snap the fingers with the five nails. (19)
On the left [hand] are the five sciences, and on the right likewise the five;
they are mounted upon horses, brilliantly radiant, youthful maidens with prominent nipples. (20)

Adorned with serpent ornaments, their hair tied in the fashion of a maiden's braid, they were led away by her who bore a sword and shield; while holding their own weapons, they held lotuses in their hands.
Their garments resembled Indra’s bow (the rainbow) and were adorned with various flowers;
they had fastened their armor around their waists and wore the lords of serpents as upper cloths.
But Tvaritā, moving with haste, the heroic one of fierce form,
having placed [the first set] on the feet, should place the second on the two shanks.
The third [syllable] one should place on the region of the knees, the fourth on the region of the thighs, the fifth on the region of the private parts, and the sixth on the navel. || 24 ||
The seventh [syllable] should be placed in the heart; the eighth in the region of the throat;
the ninth is placed in the mouth; and the tenth one should place upon the head.
Thus, with his body thus armored, the king, desiring victory, shall conquer the kingdoms of others and return again unharmed. (26)
Free from obstacles, the practitioner shall swiftly cause all accomplishments to be bestowed.
Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) according to this method, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times.
Having meditated upon the goddess Tvaritā, one shall accomplish even that which is difficult to achieve.
Thus ends the third chapter in the *Ādya-troṭala-mahātantra*, the *Tvaritā-mūlasūtra*. 3.
Now I shall explain the mudrās which bestow all accomplishments;
when accompanied by these mudrās, the goddess Tvaritā becomes the granter of success. (1)
She quickly becomes present and accepts the worship as well;
therefore, O bird, listen with a one-pointed mind as I shall explain the mudrās. (2)
The *praṇītā* is said to be fivefold; I shall describe the blind one among them:
having joined the two hands together, one should press the two thumbs in the middle. (3)
One should place the two index fingers joined at the head upon that [object] above the crown;
this is declared to be the *praṇītā* [mudrā], which one should bring to the region of the heart.
The little finger is raised while the middle fingers are joined; those who know this mudrā call it *viduḥkhaga*.
Having placed the index fingers in the middle, they should touch each other at the mouth.
One should place the tips of the two middle fingers in the center; this is proclaimed as the *bhedinī* [mudrā].
Having bound that [mudrā] at the region of the navel, one should then extend the two thumbs upward.
The Karālī-mahāmudrā should be applied at the heart by the practitioner;
then, having bound it again as before, one should raise the two thumbs.
She is proclaimed as Vajratuṇḍā; one should bind her at the region of the face.
With both hands, one should bind her at the wrists. (8)
The three [fingers] on each hand are extended; this is prescribed as the Vajra-mudrā. However, the single middle finger pointing upward is prescribed as the Śakti itself.
Having placed the fingers of both hands facing each other with their tips meeting, held at the region of the heart, it is called the staff (daṇḍa) mudrā.
Slightly bending the right hand and forming a fist with the two fingers [the index and middle fingers] extended upwards—
the middle finger and the forefinger— in this manner the sword mudrā is prescribed.
One should press the tip of the index finger with the middle finger of the left hand;
the hollow space between those [fingers] is prescribed as the noose mudrā (pāśamudrā).
Raising the left hand, the four fingers are contracted;
placing them upon the surface of the thumb, the movement of the index finger constitutes the Dhvaja (Banner) mudrā. || 13 ||
Having formed fists with both hands,
one should place the left hand downward and the right hand upward upon the right side of the body.
When the little finger is thus bent, it becomes the *gadā* (mace);
then, pressing with the thumb, the three [fingers] should be directed upward to form the *triśūla* (trident). || 15 ||
The middle [finger] alone is likewise prescribed as the upward-pointing power (śakti);
having formed a fist with the right hand, one should extend the little finger.
With the arms and heads joined together, it is performed thus in the lake;
the right hand is turned upward and placed upon the right knee. (17)
O Lord of the Sky-Goers, these mudrās of the Giver of Boons have been explained to you:
having extended the left arm, one should form the wheel-fist (*cakramuṣṭi*). (18)
One should form the *jyeṣṭha* [mudrā] above; thus is the bow [mudrā] prescribed. With the middle finger of the left hand, one should press the tip of the index finger. (19)
In the middle of those two, however, a hollow space is prescribed for the noose mudrā;
having formed a fist with the left hand, one should place it at the region of the heart.
This would be the mudrā of Hara, having turned the left [hand] downward-facing.
The finger-tips are rounded, and it becomes a bell through its movement. || 21 ||
Having formed a fist with the left hand and raised the index finger,
one should bend the left index finger and bring it back to the sixth root-position.
One should join the tip of the middle finger with the third joint of the thumb;
thus the mudrā of the conch (śaṅkha) is formed, while one should bind the fist on the left side.
Having made the index finger curved, it is prescribed for the goad;
on the left, one should extend the fingers while slightly raising them.
For this seal of Abhaya, one should again place both hands facing each other, with the fingers joined downward and the branches (fingers) pointing upward, forming a circular shape. || 25 ||
Having placed the middle fingers and thumbs together so that they form a well-knotted lotus shape, this shall be the mudrā of the lotus; one should place it at the heart.
Grahaṇīmokṣaṇī, Jvālinī, Sūkarī, Mṛgī,
and Praṇītā— these five mudrās one should employ during worship and fire-offerings.
At the times of initiation, these should be applied by the teachers for the disciples;
twenty-eight mudrās have been taught in the *Troṭalottara*. (28)
O Lord of Birds, those who desire accomplishment should always apply themselves [to these] at all times.
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the *Tvaritāmūlasūtra*, the great tantra of the first *Troṭala*.
Now I shall explain the initiation (dīkṣā) which bestows both spiritual accomplishments (siddhi) and liberation (mokṣa),
after having drawn the Vajrārgala [mandala] characterized by the previously mentioned features.
Beginning from one cubit and not exceeding nine cubits,
one should place [the deity] upon the pericarp of an eight-petaled white lotus.
With this mantra, one should unite the five-faced, most terrifying, adamantine-bodied, and mighty lord of birds with the excellent seat.
Having written "Ha He Vajra" and likewise "De He," as well as "Ghu Ru," then again "Ghu Ru Gu Lu," and furthermore "Gu Lu Gar Ja. (4)
Furthermore, by joining *he* and *haṃ*, the twenty-syllable mantra is proclaimed;
this becomes the five-faced seat of the Goddess upon a lotus.
O Bird, one should worship Tvaritā, who is seated upon this throne that pervades the entire universe from Ananta up to Śiva.
"One should know that Goddess to be present there, the swift bestower of success.
Garuḍa said:
"O Lord, tell me the characteristics of the five-faced Lord of Gods. (7)
"Vajrārgalapura is the most excellent, bringing about the presence of the Goddess.
Thus spoke Īśvara.
There should be four lines extending horizontally and upwards. || 8 ||
The wise man should construct the squares by dividing [the area] into nine parts;
the squares situated in the cardinal directions are to be retained, while those in the intermediate directions are to be eliminated.
In the corners of the middle square, eight lines for the paths are situated;
one should bring them together in the center of the corners of the outer square.
The middle prong of the vajra should be above the outer line;
the wise one should fashion the bends of the outer lines from the vajra.
In the central square, there should be a brilliant yellow lotus;
having drawn it with black powder, its interior should be white like a thunderbolt.
The outer [mandala] should be square and marked with the vajra-sampuṭa;
at the gates, the mantra-practitioner should place four vajra-sampuṭas.
The gate should be the measure of a lotus, and the pathway should be equal [in width].
With five-colored powders, the city within the womb [of the mandala] should be made red.
One should fashion exactly sixteen [petals] with the color of saffron filaments;
the pericarp in the center should be marked with a bindu and made with red powder. || 15 ||
Those who have been initiated into this supreme King of Mandalas shall certainly attain vast accomplishment, as well as both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (16)
He conquers enemy kingdoms and swiftly attains sovereignty; indeed, he brings under his control a man who has arrived at the proper time from the midst of the circle of kings.
Death does not afflict one who stands [in this state], nor do nagas, rakshasas, grahas, and the like;
terrified by fear, they perish upon seeing the preeminent one of the mandala. (18)
If one places the *ari* syllables as an offering within the central joint of the tip of the vajra, all [enemies] are paralyzed, deluded, and restrained; thus they are easily subdued. (19)
Worshipped right here, the Goddess quickly grants success to the practitioner;
she who has been worshipped in the center of the pericarp, possessing the characteristics previously described. (20)
One should establish the form, illuminated by the *praṇava*, with the syllable *hūṃ*;
having uttered the root-mantra, [one should place] the bird (the soul) situated in the space above the wind.
Furthermore, with the first [mantra], one should worship in the pericarp;
thus, having worshipped in clockwise order, one should worship each seed-syllable starting from the beginning.
Within [the mandala], however, the limbs of the Vidyā are placed starting from the southeast up to the seat;
the Eye is in the center, the Weapon is in the cardinal directions, and this is the characteristic for the secret paths.
Starting from the east and turning clockwise, the weapons are located from the center of the eyes;
the messengers are situated on the left and right sides of the four filaments.
Having worshipped five by five with their respective names, one should assign them;
and one should install the eight world-protectors (lokapālas) on the exterior of the inner maṇḍala.

One should join [the seed-syllable] ending in the letter *va*, mounted upon the fire (*ra*), modified by the sixth vowel (*u*), and conjoined with the fifteenth vowel (*au*), with their respective individual names. || 26 ||
One should worship five on the left and five on the right;
then one should again join the limbs of the Vidyā and the secret limbs by means of the *piṇḍa*.
Furthermore, one should worship the Root-Vidyā upon the pericarp;
having worshipped it three times with flowers and fragrant perfumes. (28)
With various kinds of incense, well-prepared foods and drinks, diverse types of meat, and likewise many varieties of fruits. (29)
With liquors, streams of *surā*, as well as sugarcane juice and the like;
with cloths and canopies arranged, and adorned with garlands of flowers. || 30 ||
With jars filled with clear water, wrapped in white cloths, their mouths covered with sprouts, and beautifully adorned with gems within; || 31 ||
One should surround the mandala that fulfills all desires with eight jars;
the ninth jar, which is located in the northeast, should be joined with the *vardhanī*.
Having established [the image] upon the pedestal, one should worship the Goddess there amidst the resounding blasts of kettledrums and dundubhis, and the sounding of conchs and kāhala trumpets. (33)
Taking recourse in the southern form, one should recite the mantra a thousand times;
then, with a tenth part of that, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) for the limbs of the mantra.
Then, having prepared a fire-pit (agnikuṇḍa), either circular or square,
it should be thirty-two finger-breadths in measurement, with its excavation and rim excluded [from that total].
The depth and the width should be equal, and it should be provided with three girdles;
these should be made with two, three, or four finger-breadths according to their own measurement.
Having left aside one finger-breadth, one should then fashion the rim (nemi);
the womb (yoni) should be made according to the measurement of the rims, shaped like an elephant’s or a camel’s lip.
The largest [lotus] should be made two finger-breadths in width, not one finger-breadth;
its height, however, should be exactly one finger-breadth in the center of the fire-pit (agnikuṇḍa).
The womb should be four finger-breadths [in depth], and the vulva is prescribed as such;
the pathway should be seven finger-breadths, according to the measurement of the arm and the sacrificial ladle.
The tip should be six finger-breadths long, and the middle of the neck one-third of that;
the thickness at the tip should be two finger-breadths, with a hollow of one finger-breadth extending outward.
O Lord of Birds, the pathway should be in the middle, and a trench three finger-breadths deep should be made for it, extending both below and above; this is the support of the command.

O Lord of Birds, the support for the command (ājñādhāra) should be made six finger-breadths [in height], and the circumference of the handle should likewise be made six finger-breadths in measure. || 42 ||
The bell-handle should be as beautiful as the handle of the chowrie;
the *śruva* ladle should be twenty-four finger-breadths long, with a hollow at its base shaped like a cow’s footprint or a lotus.
The handle-circle at the tip should be two finger-breadths wide;
the sacrificial ladle (sruva) should be made with half of the womb-shape and thirty-two finger-breadths in length.
The width should be two finger-breadths and the excavation likewise two finger-breadths;
it should be shaped like an elephant's lip according to the measurements of the fire-pit.
One should bring forth the fire with the Astra-mantra and deposit it with the Hṛdaya-mantra;
one should contemplate the Supreme Power (Parāśakti), who is the Root-Vidyā, in the center of that [fire]. || 46 ||

One should perform the fire-oblation for the rites of conception (*garbhādhāna*), the rite for a male child (*puṃsavana*), and the birth-rite (*jātakarma*) with the Heart-mantra one hundred times; indeed, one should generate the sacrificial fire with the secret limbs [of the mantra]. (47)
The Pūrṇāhuti for the Vidyā should be performed once Śivāgni has been generated;
one should offer oblations with the root mantra a hundred times, and the limbs [of the mantra] ten times each.
Then one should offer [the oblation] to the Goddess, and thereafter cause the disciple to enter; having performed the striking with the weapon-mantra (astra), one should then assign the secret limbs.
Equipped with the ancillaries of knowledge, one should apply them to the limbs of the vidyā;
then, one should cause flowers to be cast upon all the knots.
One should bring the fire into the sacrificial pit and then perform the oblation;
one should offer the oblation with sesame seeds, flowers, and juices mixed with clarified butter.
With rice and barley, one should perform the root-mantra (mūlavidyā) a hundred times each;
first the oblation for the state of being stationary, and thereafter for the state of a reptile.

The state of being a bird, a wild animal, or a domestic beast, the human state, the state of Brahmā, as well as the state of Viṣṇu and the state of Rudra—in these [stages], the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) occurs. || 53 ||
O bird, by a single oblation alone one becomes initiated; thus there is qualification. Now hear further concerning liberation. || 54 ||

When the practitioner of mantra, established in the state of Sadāśiva, abides in the space of the wind (khamarūt), he should perform the fire-oblation (homa) in the supreme space; for each ritual action, he should offer one hundred oblations.
Through the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) and by union with that, one is not stained by merits or demerits;
one goes to supreme liberation, the highest station, having gone to which one does not return. (56)
Just as water poured into water or milk mixed with milk becomes one, so too does the all-pervading Supreme Śiva unite within the body. 57.
Śambhu is supremely peaceful, subtle, manifest, and the self-effulgent Lord;
he is the agent of creation and dissolution, Śiva who is both with parts (sakala) and without parts (niṣkala).
Iḍā, Piṅgalā, and Suṣumṇā are indeed closely associated;
liberation occurs in their midst through the application of the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti). || 59 ||
When the breath, having authority within the body, abides in the void, liberation is ordained.
Through the *iḍā* one performs gentle actions; the *piṅgalā* performs cruel actions.
Through the equinox there shall be liberation; at the end, perfection is firmly established.
Having discerned the twilight with effort, one shall accomplish all perfections.
Having understood this, O Bird, one should diligently favor the disciples;
thereafter, the consecration should be performed with jars possessing the previously mentioned characteristics.
One swiftly attains sovereignty and eternal perfection in mantra;
for this indeed destroys misfortune and brings about the ascent of good fortune. (63)
One without a son obtains sons; one who is unfortunate becomes fortunate;
and in the midst of a thousand women, she shall attain the status of a great queen.
The mantras will quickly attain accomplishment through the grace of the teacher's status.
Then, one should dismiss the goddess and withdraw the maṇḍala. (65)

One should not withdraw the mantras; rather, one should cause the officiant to receive the food offering (naivedya), and having offered the remainder according to the prescribed rule, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa).
By this method of yoga, whatever occurs on the ninth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha,
or on the two [ninth days] of the dark fortnights of Caitra and Āśvayuja— || 67 ||
On the ninth day and so forth, a woman whose feet are wet with blood,
her body smeared with red lac, should enter [the ritual space] up to her neck.
Then, while recollecting the mantra of the Goddess, the high-minded one should cast [the offering] at night with the blood of a buffalo or a goat that is free from passion. (69)
One should worship the Goddess according to the prescribed rite with various kinds of fruits and edible foods,
with many beautiful garments, and with the sounds of singing and musical instruments.
One should offer oblations of parched grain mixed with ghee, combined with sesame and rice;
in this manner, one should cause sacrificial fire-pits to be prepared in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
The guides there continue to call out until midnight has passed;
when midnight has arrived, the practitioner of mantra should sprinkle [the site] with blood.
By means of that very well-blazing mantra, the king [destroyed] his own horses, chariots, and men,
as well as various weapons and the entire inner apartment.
One should sprinkle with that blood those who are not to be slain when in danger from enemies;
for those who have entered the Great Joy (mahāharṣa), the Goddess herself provides protection.
Invincible against all weapons, the powerful conquer their enemies.
Then, at the time of dawn, one should perform worship according to one's ability. (75)
[He should honor] preceptors, practitioners, Brahmins, dear friends, and his own kinsmen;
as well as the poor, the helpless, the physically disabled, children, the elderly, and ascetics.
Having worshipped the maiden, one should present the weapon on that day;
whatever was used for the worship, one should cause to be given to one's own officiant.
Thus, by means of these nine methods, he [should conquer] the earth consisting of nine divisions,
extending to the edge of the oceans and filled with frogs.
One should daily perform one hundred oblations with barley, wheat, and rice,
as well as sesame seeds, honey, clarified butter, milk, and likewise fruits and sugar.
Vilva fruits, kadamba flowers, lotuses, kiṃśuka blossoms, karavīra, javā, and jātī flowers, as well as various kinds of edible foods. || 80 ||
One should daily offer eight hundred oblations of fruits mixed with clarified butter,
and having performed worship day after day, one should recite the mantra one thousand times.
He certainly attains sovereignty and the desired perfection of mantra;
by remembering [this] at the three times of day, the power of the qualities arises.
If he remembers the goddess Dhanadā for the sake of enjoyment and liberation,
he should perform the recitation one hundred and eight times daily, provided he remains focused on her.
Even for him, the Yakṣa Dhanada may grant wealth from the Goddess's domain,
provided he performs worship on that day or even remembers her once a day. (84)
In his house, the wish-fulfilling cow always remains present;
having offered oblations five, seven, eight, nine, or ten times, she becomes manifest. || 85 ||
Through the yoga of constant application, Śrī becomes perceptible;
[this occurs] by means of a hundred, fifty, or one-third of oblations consisting of sesame seeds and clarified butter. (86)
The Goddess shall always and eternally be manifest before him, granting his desires; she bestows vast enjoyments and whatever else he may long for. (87)
This auspicious knowledge is all-pervading and consists of all the gods;
it resides in the hearts of all scriptures, as well as in the Siddhānta, Vāma, and Dakṣiṇa traditions.
One should worship with a mixed disposition of duality and non-duality;
one succeeds in every state without a doubt, of this there is no uncertainty. || 89 ||
All mantras in the Left and Right Tantras become tranquil;
practitioners of mantra quickly attain accomplishment through the worship of Tvaritā. (90)
And all the Bhairavas, possessing fierce, violent, and terrifying prowess, tremble before him as Śrī stands facing him on his left and right.
May the commands of Tvaritā be swiftly accomplished; may they be successful and granters of perfection.
This auspicious Vidyā consists of all knowledge and is composed of all splendor. 92.
For she consists of all the gods and stands pervading everything;
herein resides Śiva himself in his subtle form, Sadāśiva, the Lord of Umā. (93)
Śakti, Garuḍa, Viṣṇu, and Brahmā are established there;
the Sun is situated within the mass of radiance, for he is the radiant power of them all.
The hundred Rudras, the greatly radiant world-protectors, the Śaktis, the Bhairavas of fierce form, and the Bhairavīs, the mothers of Yoga; || 95 ||
The Yoginīs are also of three kinds: divine, those born in the sky, and those born on earth;
they are Guhyakās, Kinnarīs, Dūtīs, Lāmās, Śākinīs, and Pūtanās. 96.
Kiṅkaras, Rākṣasas, Vetālas, Nāgas, Yakṣas, Grahas, and others, as well as Bhūtas, Pretas, and Piśācas—these hosts are established here. || 97 ||
The ṛṣis, apsarases, siddhas, gods, gandharvas, kinnaras, daityas, vidyādharas, as well as the lunar grahas and the stars; || 98 ||
The Vidyā consisting of the entire universe is Tvaritā, the bestower of swift accomplishment;
she is Durgā, Umā, Sarasvatī, Lakṣmī, and Kātyāyanī. (99)
Kālī, Mahākālī, Bhadrakālī, Maṅgalā, Nityā, and Yogeśvarī are situated in the fourfold and ninefold [arrangements]. || 100 ||
Jayā, Vijayā, Jayantī, Aparājitā,
Raktā, Carcikā, the Vidyā Pecikā, and Karālinī. || 101 ||
Bhadrā, Yoginī, Caṇḍākṣī, Vimboṣṭhī, Kuṣmāṇḍī, Revatī, Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, and likewise Vaiṣṇavī. || 102 ||
Vārāhī, Vāsavī, Āgneyī, and likewise Vāyavī; Vāruṇī, Mahāyakṣī, Rākṣasī, and Vīranāyikā. || 103 ||
She is Vāgīśvarī, Gaurī, Cāmuṇḍā, and Bhairavī;
she is Abhinandā, Sunandā, Nandā, and Bhramaravāsinī. || 104 ||
Tārā, Sarasvatī, Ambā, Bhūtamātā, Kuṇḍalī, Mahāmāyā, Svadhā, Svāhā, Jvālā, Uṣmā, Śrī, and Kalā. (105)

She is Gāyatrī and Sāvitrī, the Mother of the Great Hosts of Mothers (Mahāmātṛgaṇāmbikā), the Mother of the Three Worlds, the Sovereign of the Universe, the Sustainer of the World, both the Supreme and the Non-Supreme. 106.
Established as living beings in both the stationary and the moving,
that earth, composed of the five elements, resides within the solid.
In the element of water she is fluid, for she is indeed possessed of brilliance;
in the element of air she is of a mobile form, pervading everything in an instant.
In the state of space, she is of the nature of emptiness, established in the void;
she abides in the principle of action beginning with speech, and her purity resides in the subtle elements (*tanmātra*).
But in the threefold instrument, the Goddess is well-established in the three qualities (guṇas).
Prakṛti resides in the principle of Śiva (śivatatva), consisting of Ananta and the others, and having Śiva as her essence. (110)
The Vidyā abides pervading everything, in both the manifest and the unmanifest state;
thus the Blessed Goddess is omnipresent and the bestower of all accomplishments.
This supreme, swift accomplishment is not to be given to just anyone;
it has been declared by me for your benefit, and one who violates the sacred pledge (samaya) should not bestow it.
It should be given to one who is devoted to the guru and intent on devotion to Śiva;
[it includes] the property of the deity, the property of the guru, and the property of Caṇḍeśvara. (113)
One should diligently relinquish whatever wealth belongs to the practitioner and the preceptor;
one should also avoid the wealth of a woman who is without a protector and that of a prostitute. || 114 ||
One should never covet the wealth of Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas;
nor should one eat without having first honored the Śiva-yogin and the Yoginīs. 115.
One should not cause suffering to teachers, practitioners, yoginīs, and mantra-reciters, nor should one ever misappropriate their property. (116)
One should not seek out others' faults and should remain equanimous toward pleasure and pain;
for the wise man, suffering and torment do not strike him, nor do they cause him to turn back from his path.
Indeed, by harming them, one becomes a destroyer of the samaya;
the mantra will not succeed at all in the Vāma, Dakṣiṇa, or Siddhānta systems.
The mantras undergo corruption; O Bird, I shall not be the protector.
One should never slaughter an animal that is devoid of the gods, the fire, and sacrifice. (119)
It should not be given to one who has not been initiated, nor to one devoted to external scriptures,
nor to those scorched by the science of logic, nor to the deceitful or the malicious.
This supreme Troṭala Tantra must not be given to an atheist, nor to one who is unkind, nor to one who delights in the faults of others; it should not be given to these.
It should be given to one who knows the samaya; having conferred initiation, one should cause it to be bestowed.
One who is well-initiated and consecrated, and impelled by the command of the guru. || 122 ||

One who possesses the true realization of the meaning of the scriptures heard, who is well-accustomed to the nature of the *lakṣa-mantra*, being free from disease, should recite the supreme mantra after having worshipped the Guru according to one's ability. (123)
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the *Tvaritāmūlasūtra*, the great tantra of the first *Troṭala*. 5.
Now, for one who is thus engaged in the prescribed rite, perform the ritual touching of the sacred field in mountain caves,
fortresses, caverns, hollows, and mountain torrents.
In a delightful and beautiful forest, at the confluence of rivers or on the great ocean, or in a most terrible cremation ground, or nearby in a cluster of lotuses; || 2 ||
In a place adorned with the Śrīvṛkṣa tree, in a secluded spot by a body of water,
or in a place abounding with milk-exuding trees— wherever the mind finds delight.
In a city, a town, or a village crowded with people devoted to the Śiva-dharma, the ground should slope toward the northeast; there the ritual touching [of the site] should take place. || 4 ||

There, one should bury eight hundred and one stakes made from milk-tree wood, consecrated by the female messengers (dūtīs), in the cardinal directions, with their tips pointing downward and their bases upward.
In that place, the practitioner of mantra should establish a dwelling and recite the mantra;
otherwise, the practitioner will be afflicted by many obstacles.
When the field has been pinned down, the practitioner of mantra does not encounter any obstacle—whether divine or non-divine, or those arising from thieves, kings, or common people. (7)
No fear whatsoever arises from tigers, serpents, water, or fire; indeed, with a mind free from doubt, one shall attain all desires through recitation. || 8 ||
Having made oneself, the mind-mantra, and likewise Śiva and Śakti, into a single unified state (lolībhūta), one attains success; of this there is no doubt.
One should contemplate within the heart this pericarp in the form of a point;
by beholding that supreme moonlight, divine knowledge arises. (10)
Having recited it one hundred thousand times, one becomes the lord of the ocean at death;
by doubling that number, one shall obtain a kingdom endowed with virtues and sovereignty.
With the threefold [mantra], one beholds the goddess Yakṣiṇī, who can assume any form at will;
together with her, the great hero sports for an excellent eon.
By means of four qualities, one goes to the state of Brahmā and reaches the city of Brahmā;
by five qualities, the state of Viṣṇu is attained and the eternal station is reached. (13)
Through the sixfold method, one attains great siddhi and the state of Yogeśvarī;
becoming like her, a Khecarī, one sports as a lord in the world.
By reciting it seven times, the wise one attains the state of Rudra and reaches the station of Rudra;
by reciting the Vidyā eight times, he goes to the god Sadāśiva.
O Tārkṣya, having recited this knowledge that leads to Nirvāṇa nine times,
one who is liberated from both merit and demerit attains the supreme and unsurpassed liberation.
For your benefit, I have declared this path to liberation which accomplishes all goals;
by knowing and reciting it, one shall never again undergo birth.
They indeed go to the supreme station, having gone to which they do not return;
she is the sole hero, possessed of great heroism, for she alone bestows accomplishment.
For the benefit of human beings, this vidyā has been brought down into the mortal realm; when recited even once, one is liberated from excrement, urine, and other such impurities.
By reciting this vidyā ten times, it becomes a purifier of the body;
by reciting the Vidyeśa [mantra] one hundred times, one obtains the fruit of all sacred fords (tīrthas).
By reciting it one thousand times, one is indeed liberated from minor offenses (upapātaka);
but by what means is a person whose soul is joined with great sins (mahāpātaka) liberated from their marks? (21)
What is the use of saying much more here? By whom could this expansion of the treatise be [completed], after he has destroyed the entire three worlds, including the gods, asuras, and humans? (22)

When the arrows have been discharged and seen [to be spent], the practitioner, the best among men, having recited nine hundred thousand times according to the prescribed rite, should reduce everything to ashes. (23)

Having worshipped the Queen of Gods (Deveśī) upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), or in an image, or on well-woven cloths; the image may be made of gold or silver, or fashioned from gems, pearls, or coral.
One should likewise [use] red sandalwood, śrīkhaṇḍa, madhukeśī,
as well as agaru or devadāru, characterized by the previously mentioned marks.
Beginning from one finger-breadth up to eight, or otherwise,
the goddess Kumārī should be painted on a cloth made of spun thread.

Or, by means of the *vīrakrama* [method], having drawn a single hand according to its own measurement on a cloth from a cremation ground while facing the enemy in battle, one should take up the *amṛta*.

Having offered oblations in the proper place according to the other [prescribed] method, the mantra-practitioner, having performed one thousand and eight hundred oblations of the vidyā, should deposit it within his own body.
Having worshipped that goddess, perform the recitation facing her, using *rudrākṣa* beads, or those made of silver, gold, or *putrañjīvaka*. (29)
Or with gems, pearls, coral, conch, or crystal,
[the thread] should be made of nine strands spun by a virgin on a spindle.
The recitation may be performed using rags from a cremation ground or darbha grass;
one should recite a hundred, a thousand, or ten thousand times, as the fire-oblation (homa) is likewise prescribed.
One should perform [the recitation] once, twice, three times, or four times at a time, and never otherwise.
Having performed the recitation according to these rules for one hundred thousand times, one should then perform the fire-oblation (homa).
With the flesh of buffalo, goat, or sheep;
with lac, resin, or blood; or with sesame, barley, parched grain, rice, wheat, and kaṅgu seeds. || 33 ||
Having performed the fire-oblation with *śrīphala* fruits mixed with clarified butter, one should observe the vow;
then, at midnight, being fully equipped and bearing a sword and shield, [one should proceed].
Holding the Gāṇḍīva bow and arrows in their hands, or carrying a sword and staff; they wear a single garment of variegated colors, such as red, yellow, or white.
The body should be smeared with blue cloth or with fragrant sandalwood paste; the navel should be anointed, and it should be well-perfumed with black agallochum incense.
His head was adorned with a garland of various flowers worn upon it,
and he was decorated with gold, jewels, and other ornaments, his mouth filled with betel.
With a joyful and nourished mind, having honored the Goddess in his own home with offerings of flowers and all necessary articles for every limb, [he should proceed].
Having emerged from the mantra-master's body, speech, and self— which are like copper—
the wise man should go toward the southern direction and offer an oblation at the door.
One who has been incited by the mantra of a female messenger (dūtī) should not cause the root-vidyā to be given.
[This applies] at a crossroads, under solitary trees, at a place where a ritual stake is set, or in a cremation ground. (40)
Having offered the oblation according to the prescribed rite, the wise practitioner should mutter the mantra of the Goddess;
having performed this once, the reciter of the mantra should say: "Come quickly! (41)
By this very method, through nine groups of nine, a meeting with the yogis certainly occurs; there is no doubt in this matter.
He engages in speech, sacrificial offerings, and likewise play; of this there is no doubt.
Then, divine knowledge indeed arises for the practitioner. (43)
Far-reaching vision, as well as hearing and reflection, arise;
one becomes preeminent in strength, possesses great splendor, and attains the speed of thought. (44)
He travels together with the yogis throughout the mobile and immobile Jambudvīpa;
he enjoys the entire earth, which cannot be obstructed even by the gods. (45)

One should perform the ritual practice (caryā) in spring, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) in winter, and during the rainy season, the practitioner whose mind is agitated should perform the recitation (japa). 46.
This procedure has been fully explained; one may perform it according to one's desire.
By the grace of the Goddess, the practitioner of mantra attains all accomplishments. || 47 ||
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the *Tvaritāmūlasūtra*, the great tantra of the first *Troṭala*.
From here on, listen to the *svedaprastāra*, which bestows all accomplishments (*siddhi*). It belongs to one who knows the expansion of the Vidyā and who understands the various types of mudrās. (1)
Divided by a nine-square grid and further distinguished by the *vidarbha* method, they know this supreme *troṭala*, which is difficult to obtain, as the classification of the Vidyā. || 2 ||
By way of direct and reverse order, through combined and separate application, by the conjunction of the ear and non-ear, and from the division beyond that; (3)
By means of the half-moon arrangement of the meters, there are four divisions distinguished by further subdivisions.
When his body is armored by the Goddess through the yoga of the three triads, he understands the distinctions of mantra and shall obtain the fruit of all accomplishments. || 4 ||
The applications of mantras and yantras have emerged in manifold ways;
however, the mantras established in scripture after scripture, and their practical applications therein, are difficult to find.
I shall proclaim those applications; listen with a one-pointed mind, O Bird!
These must be guarded with great effort, for they bring about immediate accomplishment.
Wicked men, possessed by anger and greed and driven by lustful desires, take away one's life; therefore, one should always protect the *prastāra*.
One who is devoid of devotion, addicted to vices, greedy, a breaker of agreements, covetous, quarrelsome, slanderous, stubborn, an atheist, a reviler, and deceitful; || 8 ||
One who betrays the guru, as well as one who is arrogant, always intent on the slaughter of living beings, and one who relies upon dry logic— these should always conceal the *prastāra*.
O Bird, one who discriminates between what is appropriate and inappropriate should cause the *prastāra* to be given.
Garuḍa said:
I have heard all the divine sciences, as well as the mudrās and the mode of worship.
By means of a secret arrangement, however, everything remains concealed;
but those who are devoid of such an arrangement are deficient in all their undertakings.
"Success in ritual action does not arise for those whose *prastāra* is hidden;
O Lord, show us favor and reveal the *prastāra* to us. (12)
"O Lord, tell me, your devotee, of the attainment of great success in action. The Lord said:
O Lord of Birds, hear how their origin occurred according to the previous creation.
In the beginning, there was a great and terrible darkness pervaded by Māyā;
from it arose the supreme, subtle-formed, and highly radiant Śivatattva.
Therefore, from the radiant Sadāśiva, the radiant Kalā arises;
through union with the principle of Māyā, she creates the power Manonmanī.
Through the power of her mental intoxication, she attained a portion of the Lord's energy;
there, an egg was produced, extending for ten million yojanas.
Deep red, impenetrable, blazing, a force roaring with a great sound—
filled with wonder, I meditated upon Manonmanī in my hand. (17)
Then, having bound the forefinger with the splendor of the Fire-god,
the hundred Rudras— possessing vajra-bodies and great strength— emerged.
One hundred [of them] were greatly radiant, three-eyed, and blazing with crowns;
they stood arranged in pairs, each pair uttering "Brahman, Brahman."
The Śaktis, made radiant by fifty divisions, abide there;
from them the fifty letters of the Mātṛkā have emerged.
But protected by the power of knowledge and emitting the resonance of the Vedas,
the universe was sustained by them, and thus it attained stability.
Having divided the *praṇītā* [vessel] with my little finger,
I have drawn forth the supreme power and joined it with the state of *munmana*.
Then, having bound the Vajratuṇḍā for the sake of the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), you shall become Tārkṣya there; thus Vajratuṇḍā shall bring about happiness.
Then, struck by the Vajrakuṇḍa, that eggshell split open;
a hole was produced there, from which steam and blazing flames issued forth.
Accompanied by the sound of the Vedas, with its face formed by the fire of Jātavedas,
that sound arising from Rudra becomes the blazing fire of the cosmic egg.
That [essence] of Soma is known as *sṛta*; that sound is joined with resonance (*dhvani*).
Thus the Vedas are fully explained; that is the Veda conjoined with Soma. (26)
From the union [of these], there arose from the lotus-bud-stalk Viṣṇu;
and Brahmā, containing the Vedas within his womb, was produced from the bud as the sound of the Vedas.
O Lord of Birds, you entered that fiery-mouthed opening;
and within that egg, there flowed a liquid white as milk.
But he who abides there, greatly radiant and resembling crystal, possessed of great splendor,
the glorious one holding a mace and a conch, with a lotus in his navel and arms reaching down to his knees, is the twice-born.
The adamantine body, of great splendor, the supreme reality and great strength of man;
the omniscient, the creator of all, the master, the devoted, and the imperishable Yamā. (30)
"Arise, arise! Why do you stand still? You must exit through this opening.
Enraged by those words, he said: "I am Viṣṇu; who are you? (31)
A terrifying battle, causing the hair to stand on end, ensued between the two;
due to that very partiality, they struck one another down.
The lotus bud within the wombs of Brahmā blossomed by its splendor;
and when those two entered into combat, a great bubble arose.
Then Brahmā, possessing a luster like the color of milk, emerged from the interior of a lotus and sat there upon the swan that had arisen.
There, the one born from the swan was stepped upon by Garuḍa;
Brahmā was seated there, and Viṣṇu was then turned into dry land. (35)
While meditating upon the supreme reality— Śiva, who is beyond death and imperishable—
Viṣṇu was lifted up by Garuḍa as he emerged from the opening of the serpent's hood.
For the sake of this offering, I have taken from the middle of my own eyes a great and wondrous mass of light, the splendor of your lotus-mudrā.
When Jyeṣṭhā is conjoined with Pihita and Rudra, it then becomes Vajraka; it is the origin of Āditya, endowed with a mass of splendor.
Śaktīśa, Ragu, Guru, Umīśa, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and Manonmanī are established there;
likewise, the hundred Rudras stand as upholders of the staff by means of their own powers.
Accompanied by the *bhedinī* mudrā, they produce the sound of the syllable *phaṭ*;
everything within the entire range of the worlds is scorched by their rays. (40)
Just as those powers born of splendor were irresistible,
so then the great Karālī, the terrifying one, was bound by Īśvara.
All the Śaktis were terrified, as were their father and the best of the gods;
neither the fragments nor the seeds were scattered abroad. (42)
One should place the Śivatattva in the center of the Egg of Brahmā;
Sadāśiva to the east, Īśvara, and Manonmanī.
Garutmīśa, as well as Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Tejo, and Vidāraṇa—
these Śivādityas, ending with Īśāna, are established within the mass of light (tejaḥpiṇḍa). || 44 ||
Their splendor arose together with the messengers headed by Indra;
from there, it pervaded the entire world in all the cardinal and intermediate directions. || 45 ||
The Vidyā established at Troṭala is always a protector and a dispeller of fear;
thus it is known as the Tantra of Troṭala, which bestows supreme siddhi.
Thus has this supreme Vidyā, consisting of all splendor, arisen;
I shall now declare its ritual application (karma) according to its established arrangement (prastāra). || 47 ||
There should be four lines extending horizontally and four extending vertically;
thus, there shall be nine compartments, with the first one located in the middle region.
Having established it by circumambulation, one should then differentiate the arrangement;
through the sequential application of the arrangement, these ritual applications have emerged.
All ritual actions are not lost; otherwise, they would be fruitless.
However, he who understands the applications through the systematic sequence of the *prastāra* [diagram] succeeds. (50)
All supernatural powers (siddhis) remain within the closed fist of the practitioner;
indeed, the entire three worlds abide at the soles of his feet. 51.
He attains sovereignty over the entire earth, free from all thorns and without division,
and he achieves the status of a universal monarch as well as the desired spiritual perfection.
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the *Tvaritāmūlasūtra*, the great tantra (*mahātantra*) of the first *Troṭala*. 7.
Garuḍa said:
"O Lord of Gods, for a thousand divine years I have propitiated you through austerity;
if you are pleased, O Lord of Gods, then grant me your devotion."
O Lord, tell me, your devotee, about the various rites according to the different branches of knowledge.
The Lord said:
O twice-born one, this entire Vidyā, when recited even once, shall cause all rites to be accomplished by the mind; there is no doubt in this matter.
But if the Praṇītā, merely increased in size, is uttered even once, it would destroy the entire enraged triple world in an instant. (3)
All the gods were harassed in many ways by the Siddhas and Vidyādharas;
consequently, the Vidyās were sealed and again subjected to the ordeal of the sacred fire.
But for one who understands the ritual through the application of the various *prastāras* according to the lineage of the gurus, success is attained; it is not otherwise.
From that time forth, that science, which grants success through the method of the *prastāra* expansion, was set forth in five divisions; having understood it, one attains perfection instantly.
This lore dispels poison, bestows prosperity, and grants sovereignty and kingship; it also confers the power of moving through the sky, long life, and the sixth state, which is free from disease.
O Sky-walker, this Vidyā is sealed by these six heroes;
now hear, O Tārkṣya, how the various other siddhis are established.
Having fashioned an eight-petaled lotus on birch bark with yellow pigment,
the wise one should draw the essence of Śiva all around upon a skull.
Or else, having gone outside onto a cloth from a cremation ground,
the practitioner should write the name within its center, situated upon the pericarp.
Having stepped upon a birch-bark with his feet while heating it with khadira-wood embers,
he can bring under his control everything in the three worlds, including all that is moving and unmoving, within seven days.
One should write within the center of the vajra-sampuṭa on a twelve-spoked wheel;
in the middle, the name of the womb [of the deity] interlaced with that of Sadāśiva.
On a wall, a wooden board, or a stone slab, by means of turmeric, the immobilization of the mouth, the immobilization of movement, and the immobilization of an army are produced. (13)
Having drawn a triangular mandala marked with the sign of a flame,
one should indeed place Rudra within the fierce Śakti and also in the three corners.

Having written [the mantra] at the root with the power (śakti), in the middle with the letter *ma*, and at the tip with the letter *ri*—all containing the essence of the mantra—one should write it upon a skull from a cremation ground or a beautiful vessel. 15.
When heated, it undoubtedly causes a terrible fever;
the wise man, having written [the mantra] with poison and blood upon a cloth from a cremation ground... (16)
In a hexagon, a staff [staff-seal] is placed, pervaded by power on all sides;
this shall kill the enemy who has been buried in a cremation ground before long. (17)

One effects the cutting of the kingdom; one should place the enemy in the middle of the wheel. One should [place] the spear situated on the rim of the wheel, accompanied by the name of the enemy. (18)
Without a doubt, the enemy kingdom will soon go to ruin.
One should engrave [the mantra] into the middle of a sword using the seed-syllable of Tārkṣya (TĀM). 19.
Having written the names of the enemies twice with charcoal from a cremation ground in a secluded place,
one should strike them with the ashes of a funeral pyre.
Within seven days, one shall subdue a foreign kingdom or even a powerful enemy—rendering them deluded and distraught in mind; of this there is no doubt. (21)
If a woman has the name of Viṣṇu written with yellow pigment (rocanā) on her skull in the shape of a half-moon and heated, she will instantly bring me under her control.
The name written on the tip of the banner should be accompanied by the syllable *brahmā*;
one should likewise inscribe it at the base of the banner, at its top, and in the middle sections.
If [the name] is drawn with charcoals from a cremation ground upon a cloth from a cremation ground on a banner, and is mounted upon a *bhūta*-tree, there will be expulsion within seven days. (24)

The practitioner of mantra should draw [the design] upon the mace at its three corners, joined with the name of the Sun, using yellow pigment (rocanā); he should then strike it with jasmine buds. (25)

Having written [the mantra] on an ashoka-wood plank, one should summon the Guhyakas and others; the piercing [of obstacles] occurs in the direction of the Lord (Iśāna), while the piercing with the tip of the trident should be performed at the end of the Vidarbha.

On a cloth from a cremation ground, the practitioner should write [the mantra] with the charcoal of a cremation ground; he should then strike it with *karavīra* flowers using the juice of the *dhattūra* plant. (27)
Planets, spirits, and piśācas cause fevers to arise at that very moment;
one should employ the Vidyā-mantra through the messenger (dūtī) according to their respective divisions of karma.
I shall now declare the ancillaries of the Vidyā, by which one is employed in various rites:
the Heart-mantra is used in eight lotuses for rituals such as pacification (śānti) and nourishment (puṣṭi).
In the rite of subjugation and attraction, one should employ skulls;
in rites of piercing and cutting, as well as in slayings, the head [of the skull] should be used.
