Having inscribed the name of the enemy within a six-cornered mandala,
one should place it upon the skulls of women at their hair-tufts and on half-moons.
When combined with *rocanā*, one should instantly extract [the essence] from what has been struck;
likewise, one should take eight stakes made from a milk-tree, consecrated with the *kavaca* mantra. (32)
The mantra-practitioner, having consecrated [the site], should proceed quickly; whether at home or on the road, no obstacle arises.
Or, one who knows the ritual procedure should perform every protection with the Astra-mantra.
The *tāraka* is designated as the eye; one should employ it for rites of pacification (*śānti*) and nourishment (*puṣṭi*).
One should draw an eight-petaled lotus on either a skull or a birch-bark leaf. (34)
One should draw [the deity] with deep red and yellow pigment (rocanā) according to the directions;
joined with the names of the secret limbs, one should heat it in a fire of khadira wood.
Treading upon a birch-bark leaf with the foot, the wise practitioner should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times.
He should bring the gods and the Daityas, as well as the Siddhas and Vidyādharas.
Yakṣas, rākṣasas, and piśācas become submissive servants;
however, in a triangle [diagram] there is fever and burning, while in a hexagon there is cutting and killing. (37)
Furthermore, in the Khaḍga [yantra] this very same [result occurs], while in the Ardhacandra it brings about nourishment (pauṣṭika);
in the Dhvaja, peace (śānti) quickly comes to pass, or else there will be eradication (uccāṭana). || 38 ||
It may effect the immobilization of a mace and the accomplishment of the rites of the Guhyakas;
with spears dedicated to the gods, women cause terror. (39)
The messenger should be joined with the mantra, as well as the ritual action of the messengers;
indeed, whatever rite pertains to the secret limbs and whatever belongs to the messengers [should be performed]. (40)
And that Vidyā is bound within the triple-triads, established as a single aggregate;
it is proclaimed as having three parts, each part further divided, and is sealed with the mudrā.
O Sky-goer, that Vidyā is established with three [syllables] at the beginning, three in the middle, and three at the end;
furthermore, it is sealed by three other mudrās.
The Piercer, the Vajra-beaked, and Karālī as the third—
by means of their arrangement, she is perfected through manifold varieties of form. (43)
In the southeast is Vajratuṇḍā, established by three seed-syllables;
she causes burning, parching, and fever in an instant. || 44 ||
Karālī is likewise established in the south-west with three [powers]:
cutting, piercing, and the state of being beyond the mind (unmanīkaraṇa). || 45 ||
In the northeast (Sāmīra), the Praṇītā [vessel] with three [spokes] is for the purpose of causing enmity and eradication;
in the northeast (Īśāna), that which pierces it is likewise situated there with three [spokes].
The pinning down of an enemy kingdom, its overthrow, and likewise its destruction—one should thus bring down these three groups of missiles with the rightward (apasavya) movement. || 47 ||

The *karṣaṇī* [line] of the weapons should be at the feet, while the *mohakarī* [line] should be in the middle; by means of the sequential yoga of worship, there should be two or three circumambulations.
In the sequence beginning with the east, according to the order of the mudrās, there are:
dancing, piercing, cutting, binding, and causing to speak. (49)
In this manner, with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasa-vya), one should offer three oblations to the stone, the wind, and the water, as well as to lightning.
Then, one should contemplate the manifest knowledge that arises from the mind; it is terrifying, it pierces, and in an instant, it binds.
The enemy troops behold the practitioner in his embodied form as a terrifying mass of splendor, a great and wondrous phenomenon arising from the sequence of Karālī. (51)
All enemies behold her and flee terrified in the ten directions;
thus, O Lord of Birds, that goddess is surrounded by seven [other] goddesses.
Equipped with various weapons, the host of Maruts moved through the sky;
they effected the piercing of the seeds and the fourfold breaking of the seals.
A wise man who crosses over the Yopā river will conquer Śakra along with the gods, Daityas, and even the hosts of Yakṣas and Rākṣasas, even if he is alone. 54.
He conquers in battle in an instant the Nāgas, Vidyādharas, Gandharvas, and the armies of kings; he enjoys a kingdom free from all thorns.
A wise person should draw this "Sannacakra" on a sixteen-spoked wheel;
one who wears it placed there will achieve victory in battle and in gambling.
By wearing this discus, one brings about the delusion, the paralysis, and the defeat of all enemies; thus, the army of the foe is conquered.
A peg made from a milk-tree (kṣīravṛkṣa), wrapped with a thread spun by a maiden and smeared with lac,
should be marked in sequence with three seeds each.
Having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, one should cast one [mudrā] in each of the eight directions;
one should place them starting from the east according to the yoga and the prescribed rule for one's own kingdom.
By means of three mantras each, using seeds from a hostile kingdom in the reverse order,
one should bury [the enemy] in iron or bone [images] in the cardinal and intermediate directions. (60)
There shall be protection for one's own kingdom even from poison, fire, and water;
and by those devoted to the knowledge of mantras, there shall be the destruction of the enemy host.
The enemy kingdom is pinned down, deluded, and deprived of truth;
it has fallen away from intelligence, heroism, and strength, and is beset by manifold calamities.
One should quickly accomplish the subjugation of even one who has taken refuge in a great fortress, though afflicted by obstacles, destructive rites, calamities, epidemics, and diseases. (63)
They protect their own kingdom by pinning down the enemy's kingdom;
he who understands this in its true essence enjoys the surface of the earth.

One should mentally recite the mantra joined with the *kajratuṇḍa* [seed-syllable], through the application of the sequence of the three starting with *cala*, from the head to the navel and down to the feet. 65.
Even one bitten by the serpent of Time is restored to growth through the suppression of the digestive fire;
this triple application of liquids and so forth is performed together with the Karālā Mudrā.
The practitioner may engage in speech and play at will;
this application, beginning with the Nairṛtya direction, is joined with Praṇītā. || 67 ||

When joined with the yoga of the sky-fire (vyomāgni), it renders the vessel poisonless and removes the threefold poison; however, by means of reverse order (viloma), that very same [yoga] acts in the opposite way.
If one joins the head to the foot, one becomes free from poison;
having bound the piercing [mudrā] starting from the east, the bitten person shall be staked [immobilized]. (69)
One should employ Vajrā, who possesses blazing fire, in an instant even against Nāgas, Rākṣasas, Yakṣas, Piśācas, Bhūtas, and Sākinīs.
One should avoid seizing elephants, tigers, horses, kings, men who are well-prepared for battle,
large vehicles such as carts, and even small boats.
Residing within the body, it blocks the path of the three channels and accomplishes [its purpose] in an instant;
this application of Īśāna and the others is performed together with the Inī-mudrā. (72)
One should seal all foreign kingdoms; of this there is no doubt.
One should shatter foreign kingdoms and cause them to be broken down at that very moment. (73)
The practitioner of mantra situated in the fire and space [elements] shall accomplish all difficult tasks;
by the conjunction of Īśāna and the others with the fire [element], there is the cutting of weapons by Karālī.
At that time, one should maintain one's wrath; it can even slay the thirty gods.
This yoga, beginning with Uttarā, wards off all knots.
One shall certainly sever all fetters even while remaining bound;
this is the ritual application beginning with Vāyavya, accompanied by the Vajratuṇḍā mantra. (76)

O Bird, for a practitioner who has been bitten by the God of Death, there is the rite of immobilization and possession; or [the rite] joined to a staff, sandals, or an umbrella, performed one hundred and eight times. (77)
He goes to the sacred ford together with his merit and does not abandon his life-force;
from the southwest (Nairṛtya) up to the wind (Vāyu), this brings about the summoning of the Nāgas.
Having painted the Yoginī on a cloth, one should strike her with *jāti* flowers;
she arrives in an instant and becomes a bestower of wealth and a granter of desires. (79)
This threefold application beginning with Yāmya brings a Yakṣa maiden under one's control;
this application beginning with Dahanā attracts a Śākinī in an instant.
In whatever place the hero performs the recitation, he should do so together with the Karālī mudrā;
from the southeast (āgneya) up to the end of the three petals, he should recite while employing the Karālī mudrā.
One should quickly show [the deity] to a clear mirror, or to the thumb of a sword, or to a lamp; when questioned, they reveal all matters.
When applied to the three locations starting from Īśāna and ending at Nairṛtya, this [mantra] known as Praṇītā destroys the seizing spirits (grahas) in an instant. (83)
Burning with distress, they flee, abandoning their alms-bowls;
[the practice] beginning with *cala* and ending with *idana* is applied to these three places.
Indeed, this Piśācikā is designated as "Exalted"; having drawn her upon a cloth, or having drawn her on a wall with charcoal from a cremation ground, one should then strike her. (85)
By means of funeral ashes, one becomes a master of the [eight] great powers within seven days; one should bind the thunderbolt-tipped [noose] starting from the southwest and ending in the northeast.
While the mantra-practitioner recites the mantra, Garuḍa shall bring the nāgas;
these will become granters of all desires to the practitioner, without a doubt. (87)
When the four fingers beginning with the middle one on the right hand are joined in the *bhedinī* mudrā, possession by wood or stone occurs, as does possession by one's own [inner] self. 88.
From Madhya until Vāruṇī, accompanied by Vajratuṇḍā, it destroys diseases such as leprosy; of this there is no doubt. || 89 ||
From the center to the north, Karālī shall conquer the Bond;
she shall protect her own knowledge when the opponent is Śiva. (90)
One should protect oneself, indeed, and restrain one's own power,
starting from the center up to the northeast (aindra), together with the Bhedinī mudrā.
One should cut through the mantras of others and render poison into a state of being poisonless;
having placed [the mantra] within the fire-goddess and the sky-farer, one should strike down all the wicked.
The sequence beginning with Yāmya and so forth, arranged in reverse order, joined with the *vajrasampuṭa* in the center;
having placed the name in the middle, this destroys the reservoir of water. (93)
Then, [the practitioner] should place Vāruṇī and the others in the middle and on the petals of the treasury;
by this, the mantra-practitioner undoubtedly attains purity or impurity in an instant. (94)
From the gentle [Saumya] to the middle [Madhyama], heaviness arises in the jar;
from the eastern [Pūrva] to the middle, it produces lightness in an instant. (95)
The first rite is performed with the Koṣṭhaka [mudrā], while the second is performed with the Vyomaga;
one should employ the Praṇītā and Vajratuṇḍa mudrās therein.
Bheda, Tejas, Śiva, Śakti, and Īśvara— these five are applied with poison and blood to the iron vessel in the vajra-maṇḍala.
One should interlace the name with the sequence beginning from the east (and proceeding clockwise) in the center;
by this, even the Lord of Waters himself would be consumed, were he not already pure.
Īśa, Sadāśiva, Viṣṇu, and Tārkṣya as the fifth—
these should be inscribed with yellow pigment (gorocanā) upon birch bark within the circle of Varuṇa.
The knower of mantras, having placed a lump of clay upon the potter’s wheel in the center, should cast it into the middle of the pitcher; thus, a divine pillar will certainly come into being.

Having written [the mantra] with yellow pigment (rocanā) on birch bark, one should meditate upon the diamond-mandala (vajramaṇḍala) situated within it; then all the gods, carrying fire, shall cause divine pillars to arise through their splendor.
One should demonstrate the secret limbs through the gestures (*saṃjñā*) of the female messengers (*dūtī*);
by treading upon and holding fast to that [opponent], a person conquers in gambling. (102)
Tārkṣya, Śakti, Śiva, Tejas, and Brahmā—these five, O bird, having taken recourse to the opening of the fissure, one should recite [the mantra] with the Bhedinī mudrā. 103.
Having become a sky-walker (khecara) stationed upon the fire, one should cast everything at the door;
the maiden dwelling in the netherworld (pātāla), terrified, will quickly depart.
Taking [the disciple] by the hand, they enter and sport for an excellent eon.
The practitioner of mantra should recite [the mantra] while resting in a divine abode; he will attain success, of this there is no doubt. (105)
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva are always present there; the practitioner, with a steady mind, [should perform] the piercing of their distinctions upon the corpse whose limbs are uninjured. 106.
Standing in the center of the vajra-maṇḍala, one should recite the mantra of Sahakārālī;
in an instant, the tongue, a sword, or a pill will emerge.
Alternatively, if one always takes that cloth from a corpse while it is still there, one becomes invisible; this very distinction is seen by those possessing supernatural powers.
Mounted upon the skin of its foot, one may traverse Jambudvīpa in an instant;
when applied as collyrium for the eyes, that same skin is the perfected ointment that grants the power of vision.
The Lord is Śakti, the splendor of Śiva; O Bird, the practitioner of mantra should bind Bhedinī with Piṅgalā and then recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times.
Fire blazes without a doubt even when applied to wet wood; likewise, when the fire-channel is blocked and the seed-syllable is joined within the abdominal cavity. 111.
If one who is angry recites [the mantra] one hundred and eight times over a *bhedanī* placed upon a womb, this indeed renders it seedless and withers the tree in an instant. (112)
One should quickly effect the seizing of the animals and likewise the burning of the nooses;
one should mutter this while stationed in the sky, with a recitation numbering eight hundred times.
Bheda, Sadāśiva, Śiva, Viṣṇu, and likewise Brahmā—
having made the nectar reach the sky, there shall be nourishment at that very moment.
Brahmā is the splendor, Śiva is the power, and Garuḍa is Karālinī;
the movement of the vital breaths is restrained, facing the enemy kingdom. 115.
Having recited [the mantra] up to eight hundred times, one shall pin down and paralyze the entire army, which is equal in strength to Indra, rendering it motionless and devoid of power. (116)
Khagoviṣṇu, Śiva, Sadāśiva, and Umāpati—
the minister [should perform] the exit with one [mantra], while Vajratuṇḍā shall bind.
It is for the subduing of nāgas and yakṣas, and of the grahas and śākinīs;
it is for the subduing of bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, and fanged creatures.
For a person of wicked mind, he would instantly cause [the weapon] to fall in a state of agitation;
[he is] Īśa, Śakti, Khaga, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and Sadāśiva. (119)
Standing in water up to his neck, having restrained his breath,
he brought under his control the seizing nāgas as well as the clouds by means of a hundred [recitations].
And he brings about a great rain as long as the water remains;
he is Sadāśiva, Śiva, Viṣṇu, the destroyer of the splendor of Brahmā. || 121 ||
Having written the form of Bala upon a cloth, as well as a beautiful woman and a lady,
one should fumigate it with the net of one's own liṅga-sūtras and with the first [incense] from the city.
One should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times while moving the fire through the *bhedanī* [mudrā];
then, the maiden is brought down onto the cloth in the form of an ornament.
With her, the Hero [Viṣṇu] formerly performed the abandonment of ghee;
for the sake of the splendor of the lotus, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and Sadāśiva brought about its division. 124.
One should certainly manifest Karālī among the spirits and trees, and Piśācī;
by reciting [the mantra] eight hundred times, one attains success within seven days. 125.
In his ear, however, news is told of whatever is established in the three worlds—whatever has been, whatever is yet to be, and whatever may be present. (126)
She indeed becomes his wife; he who brings mortal women [to this state] is Sadāśiva, Śiva, Viṣṇu, Suparṇa, Śakti, and Īśvara. || 127 ||
While reciting these six [mantras], one should bring about the subjugation of the Praṇītā;
one should contemplate within the heart that flower which is confined within the chamber of the Maruts. (128)
One would surely cause even the *pārijātaka* tree itself to fall from the sky;
one should honor its leaf, flower, fruit, and edible portion—of this there is no doubt. (129)

He should show the practitioner delightful divine and non-divine fragrances, as well as jewels, fine seats, and excellent garments— the objects of enjoyment for the mantra-adept— thereby manifesting the accomplishment of the mantra.

For the sake of maintaining stability during rites for the gods, the fire, or the guru, one should restrain the self and direct another [breath]; in the case of piercing, it arises like a bird's flight.
Suparṇa, Śakti, Īśāna, Sadāśiva, Śiva, and Hari, having sent [her] forth from the secret place into the sky, [she became] the Praṇītā. || 132 ||
Having raised the little finger upwards, the wise one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times;
[he should not consider] the name, the place, the direction, the birth, the caste, the form, or the age.
Having recognized him, one should quickly bring him even from a distance of a hundred yojanas;
for dispatching [a messenger], one should employ a sky-traveler, and for drawing [the soul] back into oneself, one should employ the same. 134.
The eye is the channel for those moving in the sky; its function may likewise be through me.
When the [planet] is in the middle of the Vāruṇa-maṇi, it belongs to Indra, Īśa, Saumya, and Vāyu. (135)

Having formed the *bhedinī* mudrā, the woman, seated upon a corpse, shall eat; meanwhile, the hero, having ascended into the sky, shall recite the mantra, and she will rise—of this there is no doubt. (136)

Mounted there, the mantra-practitioner gradually becomes one who can assume any form at will, glorious, independent, and illuminated by power; he [rules] over the three worlds, including all that is mobile and immobile. (137)
At the boundary of Samīrottara, in the center of Aindra, and in Vāruṇa,
one should meditate upon Karālī joined with Viśūcika and Ruddha, ten million times over.

By sealing [it] at that very moment, one causes the bound soul (paśu) to fall in an instant. One should visualize the blazing element of water situated in space, with the Lord of the Rakshasas in the southern direction. (139)
Remaining on his bed, the mantra-practitioner should recite the mantra until sleep comes, while mentally reflecting upon the task at hand through the application of Vajratuṇḍā within his heart. (140)
The application of knowledge through one's own means is difficult to find on earth;
yet everything that resides within the heart is seen in dreams. (41)
By this very practice, a man becomes omniscient;
[he attains] the Rākṣasa, the Drava, the Sāmīra, the Saumya, the Śiva, and the Manonmanī states.
By means of the yoga of the restraint of fire, one should recite the Karālī mantra for binding;
it always brings about the subjugation of enemies and wicked beings. (143)
The practitioner of mantra, his mind free from doubt, should place the mantra residing in his heart within his own heart;
thus he conquers all enemies and even bewilders hundreds of thousands. 144.

In the south, middle, and north, as well as in the eastern and fire (southeast) petals here, the practitioner of mantras should recite these six [syllables] joined with the navel; this is the "piercer" (*bhedinī*). 145.
From the emission of that deity, water possessing the brilliance of fire arises;
it is the destroyer of diseases such as leprosy and of sins as well. (146)
In the southeast, the east, the northeast, the north, the center, and the south—with one [mantra], may Vajratuṇḍā come face-to-face. || 147 ||
Having become a sky-walker (khecara), one should paralyze the magical rites (kṛtyā) incited by this [mantra] in the southern, northern, western, and other [directions], O bird-like one (khaga). 148.
Having bound the Karālinī mudrā, one should [subdue] the fire residing in the stomach, as well as Śākinīs, Grahas, Vetālas, Bhūtas, Pretas, and Rākṣasas. (149)
The nāgas do not burn, they do not faint; terrified and trembling, they cry out.
The practitioner of mantra should bring them from the side, and once his task is accomplished, he should release them.

The moving liquid is the bird (the syllable *ha*), and the power (*śakti*) is the splendor of Śiva; when multiplied by a hundred and six times offered in the fire, the practitioner of mantra becomes the object of the universal range (*gocara*).
One who is engaged with divine and non-divine women should indeed practice emaciation;
[the directions are] north as going to the sky, south as going to fire, east as going to Īśa (Īśāna), and [west as going to] Varuṇa. 152.
Facing [the fire], the mantra-practitioner should perform the oblation with eight hundred grains of *rājikā*;
by this, even Urvaśī will be brought forth while being consumed [by the fire], of this there is no doubt. (153)

When the practitioner of mantra, joined in yoga, performs one hundred oblations for the sake of accomplishment, he should offer first to Īśāna, then to Agni in the south, and finally to the middle and the north.
He shall quickly bring a divine woman overwhelmed by passion;
the power [is] Uttara, who moves through the sky, as well as Garuḍa, Viṣṇu, and the Lotus-born.

Through the application of the fire-walking rite (*agnicāra*) and a *homa* sacrifice with offerings anointed in neem oil, one causes even a beloved who is as dear as Kāmadeva himself to become hostile in an instant. (156)
"O destroyer of the end of burning, O you of moving splendor, O piercer!"—with these seven seed-syllables, one should protect the body along with its characteristic marks. (157)
When, having ascended by means of the "chest-piercing" [mudrā] during the equinox, [the breath] enters the internal chamber,
one should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times while stationed at the "diamond bolt" (vajrārgala).
A great, terrifying sound shall arise, and a most fearsome tongue of flame,
having ascended into the mouth of a corpse and consumed milk, shall depart from there.
The practitioner, having offered portions of rice to the gods, the fire, the guru, and his companions, should then begin the rite. || 160 ||
If one should eat a single grain of rice, one will arise in the state of a sky-walker;
that corpse becomes divine, imperishable, and composed of gold. || 161 ||

For the sake of sovereignty, the accomplishment of moving through the sky (khecarī-siddhi) will certainly come to the practitioner. By following the reverse order, the mantra-master shall obtain a sword from Vajratuṇḍa.
He ascends upwards without a doubt; thus one becomes a Vidyādhara.
[The mantras] rakṣa, drava, marut, tejas, bhedana, and pṛthivīśirasī [are employed]. 163.
O bird, if one touches a weapon by means of the yoga of moving through the sky, it rises up;
of this there is no doubt. Then, grasping it with the hand, one should fly up.

Mounting those vehicles with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya), whichever vehicle one prefers—whatever has been prescribed for which deity—one shall achieve victory by mounting it. || 165 ||
Then the practitioner of mantra, by means of that weapon, shall fly up from his seat; of this there is no doubt.
That city of whichever deity the weapon is the vehicle shall be mastered by him.
Having mounted the fire-element, the Aindra-bheda, the fire-weapon, and the lord of birds,
the practitioner of mantra should ascend and fly up, taking hold of the supreme weapon.
But if those seeds are recited in reverse order for the purpose of binding,
one should summon wild beasts and birds together with the Marutkoṣṭha.
Indra, Śikhīśakti, Suparṇa, Varuṇa, and Mahān—[these are the deities].
One should indeed draw a single maiden, either with red chalk (gairika) or with yellow pigment (rocanā), along with her limbs. 169.
One should step upon the beautiful woman at the region of her womb with the left foot;
having placed the slender, beautiful maiden upward and pressed her firmly, [one should perform the rite]. (170)
Struck by a hundred mantras, each containing the name of a mustard seed, she became instantly overwhelmed, rendered fearless and bewildered in mind. (171)
She will come without a doubt, well-protected by great guardians.
Pressing down on the southern little toe, one should step over the enclosure with the right foot.
At that very moment, he brought the king, who was equal to Purandara;
[he was] Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Suparṇa, Śakti, Īśa, and Sadāśiva.
O bird, these seven are the seeds of accomplishment for the *dāraṇa*;
on that first day, the wise one [should perform] the *svaliṅga*, the *sūtra*, and the *nāryā*. 174.
When the night-stalking minister resides in the city of Pañcānana, milk should be placed in the skull of a maiden, and the ritual practice (sādhana) shall take place at night. (175)
The heroic practitioner of mantra should recite the Karālī-mantra one hundred and eight times while offering grains of *śyāmāka*; thus, O Bird, he shall accomplish the destruction of sin. (176)
One should cause the gods, the fire, the preceptor, and one's companions to receive their share;
then, at that very moment, one flies up and sports at will like a bird in the sky.
And the skull-bowl, O Bird, is certainly a perfected accomplishment equal to the wish-fulfilling gem;
whatever object one thinks of, that very thing it brings forth in an instant. (178)
Dāraṇa, Tejaya, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Khaga, Manonmanī, Rudra, and Sadāśiva— these eight, along with Karālī, arise from the union with fire. (179)

The practitioner, having gone to the sky-like atmosphere, should offer the ashes from the funeral pyre into the fire for three days at the three junctions of the day; he shall become equal to a universal monarch (cakravartin). 180.
One should cause death; there is no doubt in this matter. One should employ the Name-mantra for the purpose of piercing, as well as for the Indra-piercing and the Rākṣasa-lord-cutting [rites]. (181)

The liquefier, the flickering, and the radiant—these eight [mantras] should be recited according to the prescribed rule, while covering oneself with a dark blue wet cloth and accompanied by Karālī. 182.

Having suppressed it within the treasury, the hero of the cow-pen, the mantra-practitioner [should place] that which is marked with the charcoal of the cremation ground upon a cloth from the cremation ground, pierced by the Śakti both below and above. (183)
One should step with the staff upon the navel; having stepped with the foot upon the chest, one should [place] the southern [hand] on the path of fire until the cloth is completely dried. 184.
One who is well-protected by mantras and medicinal herbs should kill [the enemy] while wet with blood;
likewise, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Umā, and the others are certainly [subdued] when wet with water three times over.
One shall kill [the enemy]; there is no doubt in this, for the ritual application is indeed irreversible.
Sadāśiva, Īśa, Śakti, Suparṇa, Viṣṇu, and Padmaja—[these are the deities]. || 186 ||
The eight seed-syllables of fire, together with the piercing mudrā,
should pervade the entire universe by means of the wind that moves through space. (187)
Frightened by the blood of Tuṣāra, extending as far as the realm of Brahmā, the supreme channel (parā-nāḍī) within the fire of the nose resembles the color of an Indragopa insect. 188.
Resembling a lotus fiber, subtle and inseparable—that is the needle-maṇḍala.
Having gone as far as the city of Soma, the wise one should recite the mantra a hundred times. 189.
Having caused it to enter the chamber of the wind, one should draw that [nectar] out very gradually;
from the center of the face, according to the characteristic signs, one should draw the nectar into the mouth.
With that divine nectar, the wise one should thoroughly satisfy the body;
and he should practice this yoga constantly, step by step. (191)
The mantra-practitioner shall become free from old age and death, independent, all-pervading, and a sovereign lord;
he attains the status of a universal monarch (cakravartin) and shall possess a lifespan of a great eon (mahākalpa). || 192 ||
Having consecrated the eight squares with the eight seed-syllables of one's own directions,
one should [offer] eight portions of sugar and likewise eight [other substances], each slowly [repeating] a hundred times.

Having formed the Karālinī mudrā with the fingers, the practitioner of mantra should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times; indeed, that same number [of recitations] should be performed with the eight seed-syllables by blocking the fire-channel (nāḍī).
In a waterless place, the mantra-practitioner should scatter ashes for the protection of the field; [this wards off] grasshoppers, leeches, locusts, and reptiles. (195)
For these birds, deer, and boars, there shall be a firm bond;
[one should draw] a lion on a stone slab, marked with a vajra-enclosure. (196)
The mantra-practitioner should quickly draw the excellent city, which delights the heart,
written with charcoal from a cremation ground and provided with a seal.
One should draw an eight-petaled lotus endowed with the flavor of madness;
having written *volomā* and *tvaritā*, one should place the piercing [syllable] upon the pericarp.
One should write all the names of the enemies upon the pericarp; then one should encircle it with the Cakravegā and again with the Brahmavetālinī.
Within the center of the Vajrasampuṭa, having drawn the eight female messengers (dūtī) in the cardinal and intermediate directions, [one should place them] within the four-cornered inner enclosure.

Just as the secret limbs are situated in their proper places, O Lord of Birds, the piercing [of the channel] should be applied in the center of the wheel-velocity, above the pericarp of the heart. 201.
Śiva is in the northern womb, while the Śikhā mantra should be in the eastern womb;
the Kavaca is to be written in the south, and the Netra mantra is located in the western direction.

One should encircle all the points of the vajras with the weapon-mantra alone, situated in the eastern and western directions as well as those extending toward the southern and northern directions. (203)
One should cause it to emerge with the tip of the vajra and pierce it with the perimeter;
Śabarī, whose face is like a vajra, is in the east, and likewise Śabarī is in the south. (204)
Plavaṅgī is situated in the western part, and Piṅgalā is located in the north;
she is the line of the thunderbolt that has emerged from the northeast.
Having drawn Jvālinī in the southeast corner,
and having drawn Karālī in the southwest, one should then proceed toward the northwest.
There, the wise one should write Manovegā, starting from the northwest and proceeding to the northeast; having written Raudrī there, he should do so with reversed syllables.
One should write all the mantras upon these vajra-bolts;
furthermore, one should write them again on the surface of a stone slab in the second [section]. || 208 ||
Having folded them together, one should bind their joints with a tail-hair cord;
then, having smeared them with cow-dung, one should worship them according to the ritual procedure.
With yellow and black flowers, as well as with fragrant flowers and offerings, one should either cast them into the midst of water or bury them in the ground. || 210 ||
O Lord of Birds, one who performs the worship of this mantra four times a day can paralyze enemy armies, as well as delude and bind them.
He may split or even slay the armies of Śakra in great numbers;
having been restrained by the adamantine bolt, they become terrified with fear and utterly distraught. (212)
With their vigor dispelled, trembling and afflicted by fear, even those enemies who were as powerful as Indra and difficult to overcome became easy to subdue. (213)
Having restrained [the opponent] with the Vajrārgala [mudrā], one leads them a single step;
the paralysis of the mind, the paralysis of the mouth, and the paralysis of movement will certainly occur. (214)
He who knows this arrangement of the five-faced one and the sealing of the adamantine bolt, O Lord of Birds, shall conquer his enemies. (215)
The breaking [of obstacles] is external by means of the protective enclosures (paridhi); the immobilization of divine beings is manifest.
One should certainly immobilize the poison of the jar, fire, logic, and the treasury; there is no doubt in this matter. || 216 ||
That which is impure is led to purity when it stands upon the inverted steps;
the Vidyā, however, is joined to the syllables of the sequence within the city of the five-faced one.
However, that which is pure burns quickly when placed in a stainless iron vessel;
or, by drawing [the letters] with peacock bile, one may bring even the pure to a state of impurity. || 218 ||
Having written this city of adamantine bolts on birch bark with yellow pigment (rocana),
one should perform protection upon the body there by means of the seed-syllables of the mantra of Smara.
Enveloped by the *tāra* during the fire-oblation, this [mantra] is of great power;
it burns away untimely death and destroys royal calamities. (220)
It is the destroyer of divine and non-divine obstacles, as well as the fears of poison, fire, and water; it is the protector that crushes fanged beasts and enemies. (221)
O Lord of Birds, it bestows success upon undertakings already begun, grants nourishment, and eternally produces good fortune; therefore, it should be worn.
She deludes her rival through gambling and in battles;
she grants sons to those who are barren and becomes the bringer of good fortune.
Like a wish-fulfilling gem, this [practice] is to be employed wherever it is appropriate;
having understood the ritual procedure according to reality, one shall accomplish all the stages.
Having described the diagrams for writing, one should draw the secret limbs and weapons;
then again, the circle of the female messengers (dūtī), and thereafter the mantras that bestow accomplishment.
The mantra of the Five-Faced One (Pañcānana) that has been proclaimed as having twenty syllables should be written in five parts within the city of the Five-Faced One.
One should draw [the mantra] with the target at the beginning and the middle, preceded by the syllable *pūrvam*;
wherever one applies it, through that means one quickly attains success.
The wise one should first employ the messenger-nāḍīs in his tasks;
having likewise applied the mudrās, he should then cause the rites to be performed. || 228 ||
One should employ Vajratuṇḍā and Jvālinī during the equinox;
having joined them with Vāmā, one should also [employ] Śavarī and Karālinī. (229)
Plavaṅgī, Manovegā, and likewise the messengers in front;
Kapilā, Raudrī, and Cakravegā as the third. || 230 ||
Brahmavetālinī and [the others] are indeed the four channels (nāḍikās);
one should employ Vajratuṇḍā and Jvālinī in the Vajratuṇḍa [channel]. || 231 ||
One should join Śavarī and Karālinī with Karālī;
one should join Plavaṅgī and Manovegā with Praṇītā. || 232 ||
One should employ Kapilā and Raudrī as the means of differentiation;
one should place Cakravegā, along with the seeds of the mantras, and Brahmavetālinī.
Joined with the movement through the channels (nāḍīs) and accompanied by the ten messengers (dūtīs), it is equipped with the five seals (mudrās); this is the swift determination of the divisions.

One who possesses the secret limb conjoined with mantra and well-protected by the weapon-mantra shall accomplish all siddhis, even if the practitioner is devoid of formal application (niyoga). || 235 ||
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the *Tvaritāmūlasūtra* of the first *Troṭala*.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the ritual knowledge arising from mantra.
First, one should apply it a hundred times at the aperture of Brahmā (the crown of the head).
But that fire, with two others in the middle and two others [on either side], should firmly obstruct the moon with two [channels] and the sun with one. (2)
Having blocked the location of the heart by means of the *bhedaka* [mantra], the practitioner,
through the supreme [mantra] residing within himself, [unifies] that which resides in the body at that very moment.
Impelled by the powerful seeds of vital energy, which possess great supernatural power and the nature of light,
you go through the stalk of the lotus and emerge by means of the wind.
Then the officiating priest should perform this rite with the *praṇītā* water;
O Lord of Birds, this ritual must first be performed for the deceased.
One should cause it to rest in the region of the heart and the region of the wind;
by means of the piercing [breath], one should pierce the wind and enter the body of another with ease.
Even if it is infested with worms, loathsome, swollen, cut,
or pierced by great weapons, he carries it wherever he pleases.
Alternatively, whether it be a beautiful vessel, a man, or even a woman,
once one has entered [the state] where enjoyment is impossible, one sports for as long as one pleases.
Again, by that same practice one may either exit or enter;
by this very practice, one should restrain the ear within the penis.
First, that very [point] should not be joined at the aperture of Brahmā (the crown of the head);
rather, one should place the restraint in the region of the anus and the piercing in the heart. (10)
By means of the Bhedinī mudrā, the mantra-practitioner, having performed the upward egress (utkramaṇa) of himself or another in an instant, [projects] a blazing mass of intense splendor.
It should emerge through the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra); one attains liberation that is both supreme and non-supreme.
Having gone there, one does not return; one becomes Śiva, the all-pervading.
The *tāraka* [mantra] is at the *brahmarandhra*; first, it is in the center.
Again, there is a triad on the path of fire (*agnimārga*), and again a triad on the path of the moon (*somamārga*).
Having joined the piercing [of the channels] together, one should unite the Tāraka situated in the center of the solar orb with the location of the heart within the body of the disciple.
The practitioner, having released the bonds, should not cause [the deity] to remain in the sky;
rather, upon beholding this entire world, he should perform the rite of raising [the deity] in an instant. 15.
From his own city, abiding in a subtle form, he draws [the consciousness] from Śiva into the range of perception; then, having bound the *bhedinī* mudrā and exhaled the breath, || 16 ||
Having joined the two parts at the region of the ankle of the practitioner, it enters through the path of the knots; it is split there, of this there is no doubt. || 17 ||
The knower of mantras should then apply a mass of radiant energy to the region of the knees,
and likewise to the hips, the navel, the heart, the throat, the mouth, the space between the eyebrows, and the crown of the head.
Having placed the seed-syllables in reverse order, one should bind the *praṇītā* at the heart;
indeed, the practitioners of mantra effect the breaking of the knot in the region of the heart. (19)
O Lord of Birds, by breaking the knots of the palm-tree [of the body], the mantra-practitioner perceives everything—past, future, and present. (20)
Hearing and reflection proceed from afar as protection;
one may utter all the scriptures, and divine speech proceeds.
Having pierced through the space between the eyebrows, one beholds the blazing drop;
from within the body by means of the self, one beholds all the worlds.
By the bursting of the knot at the crown of the head, Śiva becomes all-pervasive;
he is partless, supreme, subtle, and established within the five elements.
As long as one does not cause the blood to flow by means of breath control (prāṇāyāma) performed ten times,
one will indeed become self-willed and all-pervading.
Having released the bonds, the practitioner, stationed in the sky, should begin the recitation;
the hero, having gone from head to head, stands in a solitary, uninhabited place. (25)
The preeminent practitioner should meditate upon the entire Vidyā endowed with the nine seed-syllables, and recite it in its own form within his own body.
Then, upon reaching the fourth hundred thousand, it is heard that at night there is a vision;
the practitioner, having placed the mudrā upon his head, should perform the recitation with excellence.
And with a great, fierce roar and a most terrifying loud laugh,
the great secret ones, the lords of the masters of the yoga of accomplishment, arrive. (28)
Accompanied by female messengers, one should cause those formidable women to offer the respectful guest-offering (argha);
they should sprinkle water upon the heart and the secret limbs while reciting the three names.
By means of the *praṇītā* mudrā, the Guhyakas are satisfied;
he obtains the accomplishment of his heart's desired wishes—of this there is no doubt. || 30 ||
Then, once they have become invisible, the wise practitioner should recite the mantra again;
having received permission, the adept may then recite the mantra—of this there is no doubt.
But at the fifth hundred thousand [recitations], one beholds Tvaritā herself;
[one obtains] a son who is a vajra-like great hero, and the state of a sky-walker (khecaratva), which is very difficult to attain. (32)
By bestowing the previously mentioned meaning, the nine-syllabled Vidyā shall bind Praṇītā at the crown of the head, like a staff upon the surface of the earth.
Having bowed down, that goddess, being satisfied, vanished right there;
meanwhile, the wise one, having performed the previously mentioned sacrifice at every sight [of her], remained steadfast.
He should offer one hundred thousand oblations of sesame and clarified butter, along with the flesh of a ram,
a goat, a buffalo, and a human, into the midst of the fire when the hundred thousand have been completed.
The goddess is seen swiftly when one is devoted to the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti);
then, with a joyful mind and well-spoken words, one should offer the respectful water (arghya).
The hero, his heart agitated, would then perform that rash act.
Then the goddess said, "O son of a virtuous man, O you of great asceticism! (37)
Propitiated by excellent devotion, [the deity] says: "Arise, arise! Go!
Accompanied by your companion, proceed toward the great siddhi of moving through the sky. (38)
Then that hero, accompanied by his companion, rises into the sky;
greatly radiant, he proceeds toward a mass of splendor wherever he desires.
One who acts according to one's own will, being eternally all-pervading, shall attain imperishable Śiva-hood;
yet embodied beings remain as mere skeletons, nothing but skin and dried-up lumps of flesh.
But the practitioners and their followers, who had come as companions to Death, were also touched by half a drop [of nectar], being strengthened by the power of austerity. (41)
Endowed with the power of the Goddess and possessed of the splendor of the mantra, he assumed a divine form, three-eyed and radiant with a crown. 42.
These great-souled ones fly up, attaining the very difficult-to-attain state of moving through the sky;
augmented by the power of Śiva, they sport throughout all the worlds. 43.
This great power of Śiva is irresistible in all undertakings;
even in the Kali age, O Lord of Birds, it bestows success—of this there is no doubt.
Tvaritā, who goes to the heart, is swift, rapid, radiant, and bestows success upon those who are resplendent;
she is sharp, terrifying, fierce, and formidable, bestowing condensed success. (45)
Therefore, that goddess is swift, bestowing rapid success upon heroes;
in the *Troṭalatantrasāra*, however, nine supreme seed-syllables are taught. (46)
I have described to you the Tārkṣya-vidyā, which accomplishes all rites,
having understood the procedure for the nine seeds as they are differentiated by their various divisions.
Those with one seed-syllable are said to be nine; those with two seed-syllables are exactly five;
with three seed-syllables there are thirty-two, and with four, exactly eight.
With five [syllables] there would be eight, and with six, sixteen;
with seven seed-syllables there would be eight, and with eight, it becomes four.
The mixed rites are said to be two; with the secret limbs there are eight, and with the female messengers (dūtīs) there are eight rites—thus, one hundred and eight.
Having received this [teaching] from the mouth of the Guru, one obtains the fruit of all perfections;
the preceptor attains the hundred and eight rites and finds all things.
Together with Rudra and Śiva, he will certainly obtain both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
he shall conquer foreign kingdoms and rule over the kingdom upon the surface of the earth.
He who remembers the Tvaritā-vidyā, whether with knowledge or even without knowledge, becomes the destroyer of the sins of all mortals and the bestower of grace upon everyone.
(42) By merely performing the placement (nyāsa) once,
one has bathed in all sacred fords (tīrtha) and shall obtain the fruit of all sacrifices. || 54 ||
One is not stained by merit or demerit and attains eternal liberation;
for whatever consists of speech, all of it without exception, extends only as far as the world. (55)
O Lord of Birds, Tvaritā has entered into all of that,
by which she has known the supreme, auspicious Vidyā, which is all-pervading and moves at will.
For him, this entire triple world, including all that is moving and unmoving, is accomplished;
whereas, O Tārkṣya, in other tantras, I have been deceived by means of mantras and mudrās.
That which was hidden as the cause of accomplishment has been revealed in the Troṭala;
those who understand the Troṭala know it to be divided into manifold distinctions.
Impelled by my power, the Rudras abide in the Jambudvīpas;
for the sake of the welfare of human beings, they are always intent on bestowing grace. (59)
O Lord of Birds, those teachers who are appointed to offices are indeed bonds; they are to be honored, worshipped, and always respected. (50)
By whom this divine cause, the secret mantra, has emerged;
by whom the meaning of the tantra has been clearly proclaimed according to the ritual, without doubt. (61)
One should always worship that Guru who bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
for this, O Bird, is the supreme secret, the highest of all knowledge. (62)
You must not give this work to anyone without examination; rather, it should be kept most secret.
It should, however, be given to a good disciple who is devoted and ascetic.
And to him who has thus offered himself, [he taught] the supreme Troṭala Tantra;
the Root-Vidyā and its seven limbs are indeed proclaimed. (64)
The secret limbs are numbered as six, while the female messengers are remembered as ten;
there is one five-faced [deity], and twenty-four more. (65)
But the number of syllables in one [section] is one hundred and seventy-three.
It is declared to consist of seven hundred and nine chapters (paṭalas). || 66 ||
Having extracted the essence of essences that bestows excellent accomplishment from among more than a hundred thousand [verses],
thus ends the ninth chapter in the *Ādyatroṭala-mahātantra*, the *Tvaritāmūlasūtra*.
